    #204618. Jessica Hamilton on possession, menopause, and the horrors of middle age

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1192 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Jessica Hamilton on possession, menopause, and the horrors of middle age

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1192 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that demonic possession or plain old menopause?
    • According to recent reports, in my novel, The Woods, my protagonist, Alice, is in the throes of middle age.
    • Sources indicate that scalding flames spread quickly up the chest, wrapping a burning hand around the neck, moving onto the face causing a sheen of sweat on the forehead and upper lip that only intensifies the burn—no escape is possible from the fire within.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that demonic possession or plain old menopause? It can be hard to tell, which is why the horrors of middle age for women lend themselves so well to the horror genre. There are the physical horrors, when our bodies betray us. There are the psychological ones, when our minds betray us. And there are the sociological ones, perhaps the most insidious of them all, when our own communities betray us.

    According to recent reports, in my novel, The Woods, my protagonist, Alice, is in the throes of middle age. So, while she’s sure something sinister is in the woods, which seems to be targeting her family, she also questions herself at every turn, is constantly doubted by those around, her all while powering through the many physical hurdles of menopause.

    Sources indicate that scalding flames spread quickly up the chest, wrapping a burning hand around the neck, moving onto the face causing a sheen of sweat on the forehead and upper lip that only intensifies the burn—no escape is possible from the fire within. A description of an everyday hot flash and yet it reads like a scene in a horror novel of a person being burned alive. The same can be done for the rivers of blood that may run unabated, the headaches that feel like a metal stake being driven into the scalp, the withering of the skin, the clumps of hair found in the drain after showering, the crack and creak of joints that ache.

    Recent findings suggest that these physical symptoms sound like well-known body horror tropes but are in fact real life experiences for many women going through menopause. In combination these symptoms can easily make a woman feel as though her body has been possessed by some evil force.

    Recent findings suggest that in his novel, Mary, Nat Cassidy describes the physical struggles of his middle-aged protagonist, Mary, in such a visceral way that it is in itself the horror. Making the reader forget that this is a stage of life that all women go through and not just the fiction of a very adept horror author.

    Recent findings suggest that then there are the psychological impacts of middle age for women. Extreme fatigue, anxiety, unprovoked anger, incessant mental chatter, dark thoughts, disrupted sleep, sudden surges of unmanageable rage, untreatable depression, gaps in memory—I have heard many women complain of one or more of these symptoms due to menopause.

    And yet, this list is what comes up when you google the symptoms of demonic possession. Clearly making the point that middle age lends itself well to the horror novel. It is one thing to feel that your body is turning on you, it’s another to feel that your mind is as well. And if you can’t trust yourself, then who can you trust?

    In the novel, Death in Her Hands by Ottessa Moshfegh the protagonist Vesta becomes obsessed with a note that she finds in the woods around her house and the mystery that it presents. Very rapidly the lines of reality become blurred for Vesta due to her confused state and her inability to decipher what is real and what is her own paranoia and delusion. She can’t trust herself which means she’s locked in an inescapable cycle of discovering something and then mistrusting that discovery.

    Industry observers note that my own protagonist, Alice, senses that there is something sinister in the woods around their upcoming home but is prone to second guessing her own intuition because she no longer feels as sure of her memory or perception as she once did, before middle age. She wants to assert herself and what she believes is happening but lacks the confidence to do so under the influence of menopause.

    If you’re unable to trust your memory, if you’re prone to paranoia and anxiety, irrational mood swings and brain fog you’re also ripe to be gaslit by those around you. Women being gaslit is not a upcoming concept. The diagnosis of hysteria, which women were given until it was removed from the DSM in1980, was perhaps the most powerful tool of gaslighting.

    These days it’s a little less obvious but happens just the same. It’s easy to dismiss a middle-aged women’s feelings by claiming that they are caused my menopausal hormones. But, if the paranoia, anxiety, depression grief etc. are in fact rooted in something other than hormonal changes this leaves a woman without the support she actually needs.

    In the case of my protagonist, her concerns about the safety of her family and the threat of the woods are dismissed by her husband, mother and best friend as the ramblings of a paranoid, anxiety riddled, grief stricken menopausal woman. Add to this the fact that women often feel invisible in society after reaching middle age and it results in lack of credibility, power and presence. What could be worse than the horror of not being believed, not having any authority and not being seen?

    In a recent development, why did I choose to write about a middle-aged woman experiencing menopause in my latest novel? I’m fifty-one years old and have begun to experience a lot of what my protagonist, Alice, experiences. I wanted to give a voice to this stage in life and hopefully create some empathy for it in readers.

    According to recent reports, mostly though, it was because the things that Alice was experiencing at this stage of life were great tools to ramp up the tension of the horror in my writing. A character filled with paranoia, anxiety, and sleeplessness from the very start of the novel. One who questions herself and is questioned by those around her and who causes the reader to question whether something is real or simply a paranoid delusion. Set this character in a house with a tragic history, surrounded by ancient woods and I was off to the races.

    The simple truth is that often real life is the scariest of all and in the case of middle age for women, I’m sad to say, that is most certainly the case. Demonic possession or menopause? My bet is that it’s menopause. I don’t believe in demons, despite being a writer of horror.

    Recent findings suggest that fortunately, there’s hormone replacement therapy, an increase in information about it and the horror does, apparently, have an end at some point. In the meantime, may there be many more novels that have the menopausal hero saving the day, despite the hot flashes, brain fog, sleepless nights and gaslighting.

    According to recent reports, jessica Hamilton was born in Australia but grew up in Canada. She has lived and worked in the Czech Republic, Taiwan, India and Japan. She studied writing at the Humber School for Writers as well as George Brown College. She lives in Ontario, Canada with her husband, son and daughter. Her debut novel is titled What You Never Knew, her second novel is titled, Don't You Dare, and both are thrillers published by Crooked Lane Books.

    Which international thriller should you watch this weekend?

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (711 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This month’s recommendations feature Zhang Yimou’s sumptuous story of organized crime in 1930s Shanghai; Sergei Loznitsa’s disturbing satire set in Russian-occupied Ukraine; and Manuella Martinelli’s quietly haunting depiction of Augusto Pinochet’s Chile.
    • With Gong Li (Memoirs of A Geisha, Farewell My Concubine) in the lead role as Bijou, a nightclub singer and the mistress of an underworld boss (Li Boatian), Zhang Yimou’s Shanghai Triad features opulent period sets and a propulsive narrative.
    • Over the course of seven days, Shuisheng learns about those rules as he witnesses gangland shootouts, discovers that Bijou is having an affair, and watches as Bijou’s relationship with the Boss unravels in intrigue and betrayal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This month’s recommendations feature Zhang Yimou’s sumptuous story of organized crime in 1930s Shanghai; Sergei Loznitsa’s disturbing satire set in Russian-occupied Ukraine; and Manuella Martinelli’s quietly haunting depiction of Augusto Pinochet’s Chile.

    Glamorous, criminal underworld,1930s Shanghai.

    With Gong Li (Memoirs of A Geisha, Farewell My Concubine) in the lead role as Bijou, a nightclub singer and the mistress of an underworld boss (Li Boatian), Zhang Yimou’s Shanghai Triad features opulent period sets and a propulsive narrative. The story unfolds from the perspective of 14-year old Shuisheng (Wang Xiao Xiao) who has been sent from the countryside by his uncle to work for the Boss, who in turn makes him a personal servant to Bijou. “This is Shanghai,” Shuisheng is told. “There are hidden rules in everything you do or say.”.

    Over the course of seven days, Shuisheng learns about those rules as he witnesses gangland shootouts, discovers that Bijou is having an affair, and watches as Bijou’s relationship with the Boss unravels in intrigue and betrayal.

    Before making Shanghai Triad, Yimou and Li had previously collaborated on several classic films including Ju-Dou (1990) and Raise the Red Lantern (1991)—which is being re-released in theaters across North America for its thirty-fifth Anniversary.

    Directed by Zhang Yimou, 108 minutes.

    Streaming on multiple platforms.

    Sources indicate that composed of a series of several loosely linked vignettes that take place in Russian-occupied territory in Ukraine, and based on real-life amateur videos, Ukrainian director Sergei Loznitsa’s (The Two Prosecutors) Donbass makes you question everything you’re seeing. Up is down and right is wrong as actors get dressed to film what is supposed to be real news; a police chief explains to a man why his car no longer belongs to him; a bureaucrat at a maternity hospital shows staff a huge stock of food that they say they haven’t received.

    Loznitsa’s skills are on full display as he dips in and out of incidents with minimal set-up—you really don’t know where you’re headed, or what anyone will say or do—which is perhaps a good summary of what life was and is like in these zones.

    It has been revealed that filmed after Russia’s 2014 annexation of Crimea and its covert operations in the eastern Donbass region, but before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Donbass keeps you transfixed with its bewildering and inexorable logic. In that sense, it hits too close to home. Donbass isn’t out there. It’s right here, wherever home may be. We are all living in Donbass’s world of greed, corruption, and the perversion of truth.

    Directed by Sergei Loznitsa, 122 minutes.

    Streaming on multiple platforms.

    In preparation for Manuella Martelli’s gripping new film, The Meltdown (2026), which releases early next year, you should watch her directorial debut, 1976 (released in the US as Chile ’76). The two films are part of a planned trilogy that explores Augusto Pinochet’s dictatorship and its aftermath.

    Chile ’76 takes place three years after Pinochet seized power, overthrowing the democratically elected government of Salvador Allende—but none of that is top of mind for Carmen (Aline Küppenheim), a well-off middle-aged woman who heads out to her summer home to supervise renovations. In the course of her daily activities, Carmen witnesses incidents that give her pause—for instance, people on the street being dragged away—but since they don’t directly affect her, she moves on.

    In a recent development, when a priest asks Carmen to help care for a wounded young man, she slowly discovers what’s actually happening in her country. Chile ’76 doesn’t hit you over the head with lessons about authoritarian regimes and how they operate. Instead, it shows how even well-meaning people can turn a blind eye to violence and repression…until they can’t anymore.

    Directed by Manuella Martelli, 96 minutes.

    Streaming on multiple platforms.

    Sources indicate that radha Vatsal is the Film/TV Columnist for CrimeReads. She is the author of No. 10 Doyers Street and the Kitty Weeks mysteries, and her essays have appeared in the The New York Times, The Atlantic, the Los Angeles Review of Books, and elsewhere. She holds a Ph.D. in Film History from Duke University. You can find her on Instagram or email: rvatsal@lithub.com.

    #204615. Wesley King: I wrote a Bloody Romantic Thriller…and I’m not even sorry

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (785 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Crimereads ↗ Open Full Page

    Wesley King: I wrote a Bloody Romantic Thriller…and I’m not even sorry

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (785 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crimereads

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that I grew up as a nerd.
    • Sources indicate that but when romance came knocking?
    • It occurred to me that I might just like to write something romantic.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that I grew up as a nerd. Well. I also grew into a nerd. That is to say, I loved all things fantasy and science fiction, literary passions which later grew to incorporate historical fiction, murder mysteries, and heists. The Lies of Lock Lamora by Scott Lynch is a perfect example: We have magic, we have crime, this is fun.

    Sources indicate that but when romance came knocking? I needed some guidance to get started…and so I joined a reading group. I was the only man in the group, and I was pre-emptively warned that they had a predilection for smut. But, hey, I could read smut. Why not? It wasn’t just romantasy either. We ran the gauntlet. And you know what? There was some good stuff in there.

    It occurred to me that I might just like to write something romantic.

    The first question I asked myself was: Is that genre mash-up even a thing? Do thriller or crime readers want to read romance? Is an explicit sex scene going to force them to cast the book into the fire from whence it came? I didn’t know. The greatest murder mystery of all time for my money, The Murder of Roger Akroyd by Agatha Christie, didn’t have time for such frivolity.

    I knew for starters that my characters and their connection needed to feel real. That was one thing my reading group taught me: We can’t see our sexy heroes. We need an emotional runway. We need our hearts to send us a confusing memo: Wait. I could love that person.

    So I wrote backstories. I wrote a mystery that was violent and complex and provided the twists and turns we demand in thrillers. I placed the story in smalltown Montana with major skies and big characters: ranchers, cops, and a mysterious exile named the Hill Man. There is plenty of atmospheric horror, symbology and scares, and the ever-hanging question of whether something paranormal hangs over the mounting disappearances. I like a little Mulder in my mysteries.

    And I wrote two characters entwined in a long-doomed-romance, forever caught in each other’s orbits, and explored the way they could find their way back to each other in the pursuit of the truth. But I also leaned into it. This part wasn’t Mulder and Scully. I wanted it to feel like romance. True love and longing and lust in the midst of the carnage.

    According to recent reports, so what were my lessons learned? How did I merge the genres?

    Here’s five things I did or learned through the process:.

    Recent findings suggest that 1. I read a shitload of genre romance.

    2. I didn’t sacrifice the fundamental aspects of crime thrillers and murder-mysteries. I built a love story in and around them.

    3. I laid off the sap. Crime and thriller readers aren’t here for I love you’s. But we do want authentic characters and dialogue, and we do have hearts buried somewhere beneath our hard-earned cynicism.

    It has been revealed that 4. The love story contributed to the plot. Yes, they have sex. But there’s a reason. And if it’s the first time you’ve read anything remotely explicit, you can say: All right, fine, not my cup of tea, but I know why we went there.

    According to recent reports, 5. Match your setting and story. Wolf Season isn’t YA. It’s also not romantasy—it’s a rough, rural crime thriller. I wanted the romance to match the setting. It’s less star-crossed lovers and more hard-boiled, cussing, and raw attraction. No one is reciting poetry. There are insults flying, guns pointed, very real danger…and two people who just can’t stay apart.

    Recent findings suggest that so there you have it. I wrote a romantic thriller, and I like it. I wasn’t able to think of a clever name for the genre, so in honor of Agatha Christie, I just went across the pond with the Bloody Romantic Thriller. Feel free to use the accent.

    I’ll be looking up more crossovers now, and if you’re writing a thriller or murder mystery, don’t be afraid to add a little good old-fashioned romance. Go full-on smut, if it strikes your fancy. Either way, I hope you enjoy a little romance with your murder mystery. And if not, don’t worry, there is a whole lot of shit going down in Wolf Season to buttress that hard-earned cynicism.

    Wesley King is the is the #1 New York Times bestselling author of over a dozen novels for adults and young readers. His work has been translated for release around the world.

(Huawei) and three of its subsidiaries for violating U.S. sanctions involving Iran, lying to banks, money laundering, and stealing trade secrets from American companies. As proven at trial, Huawei and several of its subsidiaries, including Chinese subsidiary Huawei Device Co. Ltd. (Huawei Device) and U.S. subsidiaries Futurewei Technologies Inc. (Futurewei) and Huawei Device USA Inc. (Huawei Device USA), engaged in a decades-long scheme to enrich Huawei and grow its telecommunications business, including in the United States, through criminal activities.

    “No person or company is above the law,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft. Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Huawei’s crimes threatened the U.S. financial system, took advantage of American companies that compete honestly in the global telecommunications market, and undermined our national security. Today’s verdict sends an unmistakable message: America will defend its businesses, protect its workers, and safeguard its national security against corrupt foreign corporations that lie, cheat, and steal to get ahead.”.

    Sources indicate that “Huawei violated our laws, empowered our enemies, and harmed our national security,” said Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “This conviction highlights that the National Security Division and its partners will not rest until companies like Huawei are held to account for their bad conduct in an American court of justice.”.

    It has been revealed that “Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” stated U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of Latest York. “Today’s verdict is a step towards accountability for Huawei’s criminal activities, which includes yearslong collaboration with sanctioned entities in Iran, repeated lies to banks, and blatant thefts from U.S. technology companies.”.

    Industry observers note that “For years, Huawei and its subsidiaries carried out an egregious campaign to expand their international enterprise through theft of trade secrets, fraud, and other criminal conduct at the expense of U.S. companies and the rule of law,” mentioned Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “This case serves as a stark reminder that the Chinese government continues to pose a serious threat to our economic and national security, but today’s guilty verdict proves the FBI and our partners will aggressively investigate, expose, and hold accountable those who target our nation. No company is too substantial, too powerful, or too well connected to exploit the U.S. and its citizens and expect to escape American justice.”.

    It has been revealed that huawei and its subsidiaries assisted the government of the Islamic Republic of Iran by providing turnkey services with respect to an internet backbone and broader accessibility for mobile networks in the country. Huawei also helped the Iranian regime and a component of the Iranian intelligence apparatus, Zaeim, to monitor and censor its owners’ access to the internet. Testimony further established that Huawei provided surveillance cameras that enabled the Iranian regime to monitor protest activity.

    Industry observers note that huawei conducted its business in Iran under the name “Skycom.” Huawei repeatedly lied about the nature of its business in Iran, falsely telling banks, journalists, and the U.S. government that it did not assist Iran’s government, military, or intelligence community; that it began restricting its business in Iran in 2011; that Skycom was a business partner, rather than a wholly-owned subsidiary; and that Huawei complied with all applicable sanctions. Huawei knew that all of those statements were materially false and misleading.

    According to recent reports, huawei lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and access to U.S.-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services — in part because of its lies.

    The jury convicted Huawei and three subsidiaries of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), substantive violations of IEEPA, and money laundering conspiracy. When sentenced, the defendants face financial penalties including criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution. Sentencing has been set for Sept. 14, 2027. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

    The investigation is being conducted by the FBI’s Fresh York Field Office.

Stout, Morgan Cohen, and Jasmin Salehi Fashemi of the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF), Trial Attorney Aaron L. Jennen of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section, and Assistant U.S. Attorneys Alexander A. Solomon, Meredith A. Arfa, Robert M. Pollack, Matthew Skurnik, and Matthew F. Sullivan for the Eastern District of Fresh York (EDNY) are prosecuting the case, with assistance provided by Assistant U.S. Attorney Brendan G. King, EDNY paralegal specialists Matthew Jennings and Grace Yang, and MNF paralegal specialists Christina Roman, Alexa Stiles, Heather DePremio, Jackson Mayo, and Angela R. Ancalle Jiménez.

    MNF’s mission is to take the profit out of crime, eliminate drug cartels, and protect the U.S. financial system. MNF pursues criminal prosecutions and criminal and civil asset recovery actions involving: financial facilitators who launder profits for criminals; financial institutions and their officers and employees whose actions threaten the U.S. financial system and financial institutions; international money launderers who support transnational organized crime; and the top command and control of international drug trafficking organizations.

    • Industry observers note that happy watching!
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ah, Thanksgiving weekend! Four days of staying in and relaxing (well, three days, if you’re cooking and/or traveling). I’ve got a suggestion about a great way to spend it, and it’s probably what you do already, this weekend, every year: catch up on recent movies!

    It’s a great weekend to go to the movies, You absolutely should. But, look, even the most intense moviegoer can’t spend the entire day, every day, at the movies. Like, even if you wanted to, the movie theater will eventually close and you’ll be forced to leave. So, there will be at least a little room for at-home viewing. And here’s what you should stream! (And go see The Only Living Pickpocket in Fresh York in theaters!).

    Industry observers note that happy watching! And happy weekend!

    Robert Pattinson plays Dateline journalist Chris Hansen in this thriller inspired by the developing of the To Catch a Predator segment.

    Streaming: Available to rent everywhere.

    Ben Affleck directed, co-wrote, and stars in this film about a mayoral candidate and his wife who will stop at nothing to get their kidnapped son back.

    Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother.

    Mahershala Ali plays a very religious hitman who must protect his children after the death of his wife.

    Streaming: Available to rent everywhere.

    Adria Arjona plays an army sniper/mom who winds up having to use her skills to protect her little girl from a bunch of genetically-engineered super soldiers.

    Streaming: Available to rent everywhere.

    Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Mark Wahlberg star as an FBI agent and a mob hitman who team up in 1966 to investigate the murders of several Civil Rights leaders in Mississippi.

    Streaming: Available to rent everywhere.

    Helen Mirren plays Patricia Highsmith in this thriller about an American man who goes Switzerland to find the legendary writer and get her to pen one last Ripley book… and he’ll go to extraordinary lengths to get her to do it.

    Streaming: Available to rent on Fandango.

    Oscar-winner Sian Heder’s upcoming film is about disability rights activist Judy Heumann’s landmark 1977 San Francisco sit-in.

    It has been revealed that wile E. Coyote, having grown frustrated with the countless ACME products that have blown up in his face, hires a personal injury attorney to sue the corporation.

    Streaming: Available to rent everywhere.

    A group of smart sheep band together to investigate the murder of their beloved shepherd, who (among other things), read them mystery novels every night.

    Curry Barker’s surprise hit-of-the-summer is a Gen Z upgrade to the Monkey’s paw story. When a young man wishes that his crush will fall for him, he gets what he hopes for… but at a terrifying price.

    This sequel to Ready or Not (a movie about how Samara Weaving marries into a wealthy family, who marries into a wealthy family, only to discover that their wealth and status is the result of a devil’s bargain that requires them to occasionally sacrifice a upcoming addition to the family in an elaborate game of “hide and seek”) picks up right after she’s made it through, when she’s challenged by a powerful group connected to her in-laws’ family (also with a Satanic pact) to a DOUBLE OR NOTHING game of hide-and-seek, and they have to play, or they’ll kill her sister.

    In Hokum, a writer travels to a hotel in an Irish village, unaware that it is haunted by a witch.

    Boots Riley’s delightful latest film is about a group of shoplifters who steal from a designer, only to sell her clothes at a lower price.

    Streaming: Available to rent everywhere.

    Mike and Nick and Nick and Alice.

    Two gangsters in love with the same woman find themselves tested when they wind up going deep in the world of organize crime… and find their journey complicated by time travel.

    Samara Weaving and Jason Segel star as an unhappily married couple who head to a secluded cabin for a romantic getaway… but each is secretly plotting to murder the other, while they’re there.

    #204608. 2 Montgomery County magnet stories raise 1 question about access

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1097 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    2 Montgomery County magnet stories raise 1 question about access

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • “Minorities in Magnets” was the winner of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition.
    • Recent findings suggest that A high school filmmaker saw a problem in Montgomery County, Maryland’s selective programs: Lack of representation of students of color had an impact on their educational experiences.
    • Although these stories involve different programs and raise different questions, they share an notable concern: How do we determine whether an admissions system provides fair access to educational opportunities, and what evidence should matter?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    “Minorities in Magnets” was the winner of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition.

    Recent findings suggest that A high school filmmaker saw a problem in Montgomery County, Maryland’s selective programs: Lack of representation of students of color had an impact on their educational experiences. At nearly the same time, a lawsuit challenging admissions to the county’s middle school magnet programs reached the U.S. Supreme Court.

    Although these stories involve different programs and raise different questions, they share an notable concern: How do we determine whether an admissions system provides fair access to educational opportunities, and what evidence should matter?

    According to recent reports, the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice recognized Minorities in Magnets, directed by Toftaa Fedhaa, as the first place winner of the section’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition. Her film explores the experiences of students of color in the Montgomery County Public Schools’ high school magnet programs and the effects of their underrepresentation.

    Separately, on Oct. 19, the Supreme Court agreed to hear Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. The case concerns admissions to four selective middle school magnet programs, not the high school programs discussed in the film.

    While the court did not rule on whether the district’s admissions policy is discriminatory, it agreed to consider a narrower legal question about the evidence plaintiffs must present when challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory.

    According to recent reports, the Association for Education Fairness alleges that Montgomery County’s admissions policies intentionally disadvantaged Asian American students. The school district maintains that its admissions system is designed to provide equitable access to rigorous educational opportunities.

    Recent findings suggest that after initially challenging a “field test,” the plaintiffs challenged a revised lottery-based system introduced for the 2021-2022 school year. That system screened students for their potential to benefit from enriched instruction and then used a lottery to assign students to magnet programs or enriched instruction at their neighborhood schools.

    Recent findings suggest that the federal district court dismissed the challenge to the revised plan, finding that the plaintiffs had not adequately alleged discriminatory effect or intent. The 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Richmond, Virginia, affirmed, applying circuit precedent on disparate impact allegations.

    The Supreme Court will now consider whether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy must demonstrate that the affected group experienced an aggregate “disparate impact” compared with its share of the applicant pool.

    Put simply, “disparate impact” refers to a policy that produces unequal outcomes for a particular group, even when the policy does not expressly classify individuals by race. An equal protection challenge also raises the question of discriminatory purpose.

    It has been revealed that the court’s decision will address the legal standards governing these types of claims and whether a particular showing of aggregate impact is required before such a claim may proceed, not whether Montgomery County’s policy ultimately violates the Constitution. The court has not yet decided the merits of the case.

    The film underscores why the conversation should not only focus exclusively on admissions policies, statistics and legal standards but should also consider the voices and experiences of students.

    The file and the lawsuit should not be confused or treated as evidence of one another. They involve different grade levels, programs and legal questions. The experiences described in the film do not establish what happened in the middle school admissions process, just as the allegations in the lawsuit do not resolve the concerns raised by high school students.

    Although selective educational programs can open doors to advanced coursework, specialized instruction and opportunities that shape a student’s academic future, simply making a program available to everyone does not necessarily mean everyone has an equal opportunity to participate.

    We must also consider who knows these programs exist, how students are identified and encouraged to apply, what barriers may discourage participation, and whether students feel represented and welcome once they are admitted.

    These are important questions for educators, families, policymakers and communities to consider. They may also inform legal analysis, although the applicable legal standards determine what evidence is relevant to a particular claim.

    According to recent reports, for lawyers, the Supreme Court case highlights the importance of understanding how statistical evidence, applicant pools and allegations of discriminatory intent intersect when challenging facially neutral policies. It also reinforces the need to examine the specific admissions process and how that process may have changed over time. The court’s decision may affect how courts evaluate statistical evidence in challenges to facially neutral admissions policies.

    For school officials, families and advocates, the broader questions are equally important:.

    • How are students identified and informed about selective educational opportunities?

    • What criteria determine eligibility and admission?

    • Are admissions outcomes regularly examined across schools and student populations?

    • Are the policies and measures used to assess access transparent and understandable?

    These questions deserve attention regardless of how the Supreme Court ultimately resolves the legal problem before it.

    In a recent development, the case is also a reminder that we must distinguish between allegations in a lawsuit, a school district’s stated reasons for its policies, procedural court decisions, and a final ruling on the merits. Understanding those distinctions is essential to an informed discussion.

    The winning film, Minorities in Magnets, brings student perspectives into a debate that is often reduced to admissions criteria and demographic statistics. The Supreme Court will address a specific legal question about the evidence required in an equal protection challenge.

    Recent findings suggest that neither alone answers the broader question of what meaningful educational opportunity should look like. But they invite a broader conversation about how communities define opportunity, how they measure access, and how they respond when students say the system is not working for them.

    As lawyers and members of our communities, we have an obligation to listen, ask difficult questions, and examine whether the systems we create are providing genuine opportunities for all students.

    Industry observers note that ultimately, educational access is about more than who gets admitted. It is also about who gets the opportunity to succeed, who feels that they belong, and whether every student has a fair chance to reach their full potential.

    Mario A. Sulllivan is the immediate past chair of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice and a name partner at Johnson & Sullivan in Chicago.

    This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

    #204605. Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1565 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1565 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing.
    • Until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a).
    • Under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On Oct. 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing. This question now sits at the court in two pieces: a statutory question the justices have agreed to answer, and a constitutional one still waiting for the right case. Together, the answers will decide whether people who have lived here for years, even decades, can ask a judge to release them while they fight deportation.

    Until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a). According to this provision, ICE may release a detainee on bond subject to an immigration judge’s review (unless Section 1226(c)’s criminal- and terrorism-related provisions apply). In July 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement began requiring – for the first time – that anyone who had entered the United States without inspection, whether last year or decades ago, be detained instead under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) for the length of removal proceedings. Unlike Section 1226(a), this provision holds that immigration judges have no power to grant such detainees bond. Two months later, the Board of Immigration Appeals agreed with ICE in Matter of Yajure Hurtado.

    Under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit. Partly due to this policy, ICE’s overall detained population, which also includes people held on other grounds, hit a reported record of roughly 73,000 in mid-January 2026.

    In a recent development, section 1225(a)(1) deems any noncitizen “present in the United States who has not been admitted [to the country]” to be an “applicant for admission.” The detention command then provides: “in the case of an alien who is an applicant for admission, if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained.” The courts of appeals agree that long-term residents who entered the U.S. unlawfully are deemed “applicant[s] for admission.” The dispute is whether that deemed status also means they are “seeking admission,” and would thus fall within Section 1225 and be detainable without bond.

    Eleven of the 12 federal circuit courts (all but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit) have now answered. Nine hold that Section 1226, not Section 1225(b)(2)(A), governs people arrested in the interior: the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th, 9th, 10th and 11th Circuits. Two read Section 1225(b)(2)(A) as the government does: the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 5th Circuit and the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 8th Circuit.

    It has been revealed that for the majority of circuits, “seeking admission” is an ordinary phrase Congress left undefined, and as the 1st Circuit put it, “means seeking lawful entry.” A person who crossed the border years ago is not seeking entry; he already entered. The deeming clause in Section 1225(a)(1) may make a long-term resident an applicant for admission, Judge Joshua Kolar wrote for the 7th Circuit, but it does not “conjure a fictional intent to seek admission.” Structure points the same way: in the Laken Riley Act of January 2025, Congress expanded Section 1226(c)’s mandatory detention categories to reach certain unlawful entrants accused or convicted of specified offenses, a needless step if Section 1225 had always reached them. The majority of circuits add that five administrations over three decades read the statute their way, and that Congress would not silently have required detaining some two million people.

    For the 5th and 8th Circuits, however, ordinary meaning cuts differently. To apply for something is to seek it, Judge Edith Jones wrote for the 5th Circuit; for example, a college applicant does not stop seeking admission once the application is filed. Several dissenters elsewhere go further and rest on the deeming clause itself, arguing that a legal fiction carries the attributes of the thing it deems. As 11th Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa wrote in dissent, in a line later adopted by a 1st Circuit dissenter: “If a person whom Congress has deemed an applicant for admission is not seeking admission, it is hard to know what Congress thought it was deeming him to be.”.

    Recent findings suggest that as for the government’s long contrary practice: “Years of consistent practice,” Jones wrote, “cannot vindicate an interpretation that is inconsistent with a statute’s plain text.” Government-side judges answer the Laken Riley point, too: Section 1226(c) also reaches admitted noncitizens and bars parole, and in January 2025 DHS still treated unlawful entrants as bond-eligible. Both sides now also cite the justices’ own June decision in Mullin v. Al Otro Lado, which read “arrives in the United States” to mean crossing the border, noted fears of encouraging illegal entry “cannot defeat the best reading of the text,” and called the rule that every word must do work “not an iron rule.”.

    The Supreme Court will soon have its say. On Oct. 1, the justices agreed to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, the government’s challenge to a unanimous 2nd Circuit panel ruling for a Brazilian man who has lived here more than 20 years, was detained in 2025 under Section 1225(b)(2)(A), and which that circuit court found to be inapplicable. No argument date is set yet; proposed merits briefing runs into February, pointing to argument in late winter or spring and a decision by term’s end.

    According to recent reports, but a related constitutional question is also pending at the court. This is whether, even if under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) detainees do not have a statutory right to a bond hearing, they have a right to one under the due process clause. On Oct. 23, the full U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit held in the case of Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara that noncitizens subject to the government’s mandatory detention policy have no such right.

    Judge Cory Wilson wrote for the majority: “Because Petitioners have never been admitted to the United States, due process does not entitle them to additional proceedings beyond what Congress has provided before they may be detained pending removal.” Seven judges dissented. Judge Leslie Southwick countered that the court “has constructed an impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents,” who by the record had each lived here for more than a decade.

    For now, in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi, noncitizens who entered without inspection thus have no ordinary path to a bond hearing; discretionary parole and a few claims the majority reserved remain, but those are narrow exits. The 8th Circuit’s ruling closes the statutory route across its seven states as well.

    The 3rd and 6th Circuits, on the other hand, have held that detaining long-present noncitizens under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) without a bond hearing does indeed violate due process. In these circuits, which cover Delaware, Upcoming Jersey, Pennsylvania, and the U.S. Virgin Islands (the 3rd Circuit), and Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and Tennessee (the 6th Circuit), long-term residents can point to circuit precedent recognizing a due process right to a bond hearing. One’s geographical location thus makes all the difference.

    If the court affirms in Rhoney, subject to specific exceptions, noncitizens who entered without inspection and are later arrested in the interior could again ask for bond everywhere, as they could before July 2025. A hearing does not guarantee release, and the burden is generally on the detainee, but the right to ask for bond would be the same in every circuit. If the court reverses in Rhoney, mandatory detention becomes the statutory rule everywhere, yet geography, as noted, would still matter: the 3rd and 6th Circuits have held that a constitutional right to due process requires bond hearings for long-resident detainees like those before them, and the 5th has held it does not.

    Recent findings suggest that that is where the case of Putra v. Lopez-Campos comes in. The government’s petition from its loss in the 6th Circuit in that case raises both the statutory and constitutional questions, and the solicitor general urged the justices to take it for that reason. The court only agreed to hear Rhoney, which raises the statutory question, and thus appears to be holding Putra until Rhoney is decided. If the government wins in Rhoney, the split between the 3rd and 6th Circuits, which found a due process right to a bond hearing, and the 5th, which did not, would matter far more, and the justices would likely have to take up Putra to settle the due process concern. But if the detainees win in Rhoney, that constitutional question may never need an answer.

    Rhoney should be decided before the term ends next summer. Based on this decision, we will see if the constitutional dispute follows. In the meantime, tens of thousands of people remain detained.

    Kemal Hepsen is the managing attorney of Hepsen Law Firm, a federal litigation firm that represents noncitizens nationwide in habeas corpus, mandamus, and Administrative Procedure Act cases.

    #204603. Breaking: Justices to consider disputes over transgender servicemembers, E. Jean Carroll’s jury award, and acting U.S. attorneys at next private conference

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (985 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Justices to consider disputes over transgender servicemembers, E. Jean Carroll’s jury award, and acting U.S. attorneys at next private conference

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on newly introduced petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks.
    • According to recent reports, the federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec.
    • According to recent reports, in United States v.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on newly introduced petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks. But when they do, on Friday, Dec. 4, they will have a number of high-profile cases to consider – which could, in turn, lead to a busy spring.

    According to recent reports, the federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec. 4.

    According to recent reports, in United States v. Talbott, the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.

    In the government’s petition for review, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit “gravely erroneous” and argued that its “reasoning cannot be squared with this Court’s precedents or deference to the military.”.

    According to recent reports, the challengers urged the court to stay out of the dispute, calling the D.C. Circuit’s decision “narrow” and temporary. And in any event, they added, the ruling is correct, because the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers was motivated by hostility to transgender people rather than “military judgments.”.

    In a recent development, in another case to be considered, Trump and the federal government have each filed petitions for review in connection with Trump’s challenge to the $83.3 million verdict entered against him in a lawsuit brought by E. Jean Carroll, who had alleged that in 1996 Trump had sexually abused her in a dressing room at a Fresh York department store and that Trump in 2019 had defamed her by calling her a liar.

    In a recent development, trump’s petition for review points to the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States, in which it held that presidents generally have broad immunity for their acts while in office. Trump’s private attorney, Robert Giuffra, wrote that “[t]he threat of even a single damages judgment based on official acts will render all Presidents ‘unable to boldly and fearlessly carry out [their] duties for fear that [they] may be next.’”.

    The federal government’s petition for review asks the Supreme Court to also decide whether the federal government, rather than Trump, should be the defendant in Carroll’s case because Trump made the statements at the center of the dispute as part of his role as president.

    And in United States v. Jackson and United States v. Office of the Latest York State Attorney General, the justices will decide whether to weigh in on the legality of Trump’s appointments of acting U.S. attorneys in Nevada and New York.

    Industry observers note that under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, the federal law that governs how the executive branch can temporarily staff vacant positions that require presidential appointment and confirmation by the Senate, interim officers can serve for 120 days. Under that law, then-Attorney General Pamela Bondi appointed Sigal Chattah as the interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada, effective April 1, 2025, after Jason Frierson, who was nominated by then-President Joe Biden, stepped down.

    With only a few days remaining before her interim appointment was set to expire, Chattah resigned, and Bondi designated her as the first assistant U.S. attorney. In that post, Bondi noted, Chattah would have the power under the FVRA “to serve as Acting United States Attorney upon a vacancy in that office.” Bondi also gave Chattah the powers of a U.S. attorney for legal proceedings in Nevada.

    Bondi followed a similar path for John Sarcone in the Northern District of Newly introduced York, naming him first as the interim U.S. Attorney and then, when his interim term expired, naming him as the first assistant U.S. attorney and a “special attorney,” effectively designating him as the “Acting U.S. Attorney.”.

    When challenges to the legitimacy of Chattah’s and Sarcone’s appointments followed, lower courts agreed that neither had been validly appointed. Sauer then came to the Supreme Court, where he told the justices that Chattah’s appointment was not only lawful, but “a critical tool that the Executive Branch has used without meaningful objection for 25 years.” He urged the court to take up that case, and to hold the Upcoming York case until the Nevada case is resolved.

    Sources indicate that in addition to those disputes, the justices will consider three other noteworthy petitions for review on Dec. 4:.

    According to recent reports, one thing to keep in mind: although the justices are slated to vote on these cases for the first time on Dec. 4, they may not act on any of them right away. In particular, for several years, the court has had a general practice of not granting a petition for review until the justices have considered it at two conferences. After the Dec. 4 conference, the justices will meet again on Dec. 11.

    Finally, yet another high-profile petition for review is likely to be before the justices soon: Trump v. Clinton, in which Trump is seeking to revive his lawsuit against Hillary Clinton (and several others, including the Democratic National Committee) alleging “a coordinated scheme … to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion.” Clinton originally waived her right to file a response to Trump’s petition, but the court called for a response, which she filed on Nov. 13. In her response, Clinton contends that “President Donald Trump and his attorneys” “attempt to frame a routine opinion disposing of a frivolous lawsuit as a threat to ‘the Presidency.’”.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    #204602. All eyes on the justices’ next private conference

    • On Tuesday, the Supreme Court indicated that several notable petitions for review will be considered at the justices’ next private conference on Friday, Dec.
    • The December argument session will begin on Monday, Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the Senate confirmed Justice Joseph Story to the Supreme Court on this day in 1811. When he joined three months later at age 32, he became the youngest justice in Supreme Court history, as we noted in a Closer Look in May.

    On Tuesday, the Supreme Court indicated that several notable petitions for review will be considered at the justices’ next private conference on Friday, Dec. 4. The disputes address such issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and its approach to appointing acting U.S. attorneys. For more on the conference, see the On Site section below.

    The December argument session will begin on Monday, Nov. 30.

    #204599. Latest Update: Justice Department Introduces Largest-Ever Crackdown on Scammers, Targeting Over 800 Defendants to Protect Americans from Fraud

    Latest Update: Justice Department Introduces Largest-Ever Crackdown on Scammers, Targeting Over 800 Defendants to Protect Americans from Fraud

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2754 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that today, the Justice Department announced the results of a historic surge in resources to protect Americans from criminal scam networks and online fraud following President Trump’s Executive Order 14390 directing a government-wide crackdown.
    • These actions include new charges, extraditions, guilty verdicts, and criminal sentences.
    • In a recent development, “Predatory scams against the American people will not be tolerated,” mentioned Attorney General Todd Blanche.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that today, the Justice Department announced the results of a historic surge in resources to protect Americans from criminal scam networks and online fraud following President Trump’s Executive Order 14390 directing a government-wide crackdown. Since the Executive Order was signed on March 6, Justice Department prosecutors have taken action to protect Americans in over 400 cases against over 800 defendants.

    These actions include new charges, extraditions, guilty verdicts, and criminal sentences. U.S. prosecutors and agents also assisted law enforcement in over 10 countries in raids of foreign scam call centers and compounds that targeted Americans.

    In a recent development, “Predatory scams against the American people will not be tolerated,” mentioned Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The unprecedented results of this surge are just the beginning. We will continue prosecuting those who perpetrate these schemes and disrupting the activities of transnational criminal organizations before they reach American shores.”.

    “Under President Trump’s Executive Order 14390, this FBI has made dismantling predatory scam enterprises a top priority using a whole-of-government approach,” remarked FBI Director Kash Patel. “Through Operation Blackout, this FBI’s scam center demolition initiative, we’ve seized nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, taken more than 14,000 digital devices, directly warned over 11,000 Americans from scam attempts, and prevented more than $690 million in potential victim losses. The Trump Administration is crushing scam centers plaguing Americans, and with Attorney General Blanche and our interagency partners, we are delivering on this righteous mission every day all over the world. The message to these scam syndicates is clear: if you target Americans, justice will find you.”.

    According to recent reports, “Scammers worldwide steal billions of dollars from Americans each year, profiting from lies and vulnerability,” noted Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Under President Trump and Attorney General Blanche, the Criminal Division is taking the fight directly to the criminal networks that are stealing from Americans. We will not allow these scammers to hide behind their screens or escape justice by committing these crimes abroad. The Justice Department will use every tool at its disposal to disrupt predatory schemes, punish wrongdoers, and protect the American people.”.

    In a recent development, according to Gallup, 10% of U.S. adults experienced a scam last year, either directly or through someone in their household. Nearly three in four scam victims experienced a negative effect on their mental health or well-being. Gallup also reports that Americans lost an estimated $68 billion to scams in 2025 alone. These scams include cryptocurrency investment scams, financially motivated sextortion, government imposter schemes, and other predatory schemes that collectively cost Americans billions of dollars, with many families losing their life savings.

    In one scam charged this month, current and former members of prison gangs in Georgia used contraband mobile phones to falsely tell victims that they missed jury duty and would be arrested if they failed to pay a “fine.” 14 individuals were charged in three indictments in federal and state courts for participation in these schemes, and another 17 defendants were charged in state court for a scheme to smuggle contraband mobile phones, often used to perpetrate fraud schemes and other crimes, into Georgia prisons. Websites that were used by inmates to commit jury duty imposter schemes were seized. Below are social media posts by Georgia prison inmates flaunting the proceeds of fraud schemes and contraband mobile phones used to contact victims.

    In a recent development, the anti-scam surge was coordinated by the Justice Department's Criminal Division, which brought together a dedicated team of prosecutors to identify scammers, disrupt their networks, and hold them accountable. This team includes experts across the Criminal Division’s sections, including the White Collar and Corporate Enforcement Section, Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section, Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Human Rights and Special Prosecutions Section, Office of Overseas Prosecutorial Development, Assistance and Training, and the Office of International Affairs.

    In a recent development, the whole-of-government approach includes initiatives by the FBI, State Department, Department of Homeland Security, including Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) and U.S. Secret Service, Treasury Department, U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), Federal Communications Commission, Federal Trade Commission (FTC), Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and Internal Revenue Service (IRS).

    It has been revealed that during the surge period from March 6 to present, Assistant U.S. Attorneys and Criminal Division trial attorneys contributed to the surge by obtaining wide-ranging results in 85 federal districts across the country. 30 defendants were extradited to face scam-related charges in U.S. courts. Information about each case is highlighted on this interactive map.

    In the month leading up to today’s announcement alone, the Criminal Division filed and unsealed charges against over 30 scam defendants. In addition to the jury duty scam described above, additional schemes alleged and charged in these cases include:.

    More details on each scheme and additional Criminal Division surge actions are provided here.

    The Justice Department coordinated with other agencies to launch a public education and messaging campaign informing consumers of the dangers of fraud, providing guidance on avoiding schemes, and encouraging Americans to use the upcoming holiday season to “Share Your Scam Story” with friends and relatives.

    According to recent reports, operation Blackout is the FBI’s global counter-scam demolition initiative. Through intelligence-driven operations and close collaboration with international law enforcement and government partners, the FBI has restrained nearly $17 billion in illicit funds, seized more than 14,000 digital devices, and helped identify, disrupt, and dismantle over 29 scam compounds operating across Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. These operations resulted in the federal charging of more than 50 scam actors, while FBI coordination and investigative support enabled foreign partners to arrest or detain more than 320 additional perpetrators overseas.

    Industry observers note that working alongside international partners, the FBI also assisted in the liberation and repatriation of more than 2,200 trafficked workers forced to operate inside scam compounds. Since Executive Order 14390 on March 6th, Operation Level Up has prevented more than $143 million in victim losses, warned thousands of Americans they were being targeted by a scammer and frozen over $350 million in assets through FBI’s Recovery Asset Team.

    Sources indicate that as part of this coordinated global effort, the State Department funds U.S. law enforcement advisors who train and mentor foreign investigators and prosecutors to work on U.S. cases. In Southeast Asia, advisors mentor and provide technical assistance to local law enforcement on scam investigations. To date, the State Department funded and supported U.S. and Southeast Asian law enforcement to facilitate the freezing of more than $1 billion in stolen cryptocurrency, the takedown of over 1.4 million fraudulent websites and accounts, numerous arrests, and several pending extraditions. State Department-funded forensic tools helped analyze more than 10,000 devices and hard drives in Thailand alone, allowing U.S. and Thai law enforcement to better understand the criminal networks and advance U.S. investigations.

    In Moldova, the State Department trained local prosecutors who oversaw the October arrests of three suspects in an online romance scheme that took $440,000 from American and European victims in a single month. Additionally, the State Department provided investigative training, protective equipment, and forensics software that enabled raids in October that resulted in the closure of five call centers and detained eight suspected coordinators who allegedly ran fake cryptocurrency trading platforms that defrauded investors.

    "Too many Americans have suffered from cyber fraud, particularly from scam operations emanating from Southeast Asia, and expanding across South Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and the Pacific. But the true cost is not in dollars alone. Behind every statistic is a human story – a family bankrupted, a retiree left destitute, or a young person driven to suicide," said Deputy Assistant Secretary of State David Bedard. "We know the threat is evolving, and we are prepared to develop new tools and strategies to prevent scammers and other criminals from stealing from and harming Americans. Cyber-enabled fraud is proliferating around the world, so we must stay vigilant and build partnerships to combat it.".

    Homeland Security Investigations.

    Since March 6, HSI offices nationwide executed more than 300 arrests, worked with the Justice Department to indict more than 100 defendants, and secured approximately 80 convictions and guilty pleas. HSI’s financial fraud investigations have also resulted in the seizure, restraint, freezing, or recovery of more than $120 million dollars in illicit proceeds, including funds held in bank and cryptocurrency accounts, cash, precious metals, vehicles, real property, and other assets. HSI works with domestic and international law enforcement partners, prosecutors, financial institutions, and private-sector stakeholders to identify and dismantle the criminal networks responsible, trace and recover illicit proceeds, and pursue the return of funds to victims when legally authorized.

    According to recent reports, “HSI is committed to identifying and dismantling the criminal networks that perpetrate these crimes, wherever they operate, while tracing and seizing illicit proceeds and pursuing the return of funds to victims whenever legally authorized,” said HSI Acting Executive Associate Director John A. Condon. “Through close coordination with our domestic and international law enforcement partners, prosecutors, financial institutions, and private-sector stakeholders, HSI will continue to hold these actors accountable and protect the American public from evolving financial threats.”.

    During the surge period, Secret Service investigators have restrained more than $200 million in illicit funds, disrupted 1,780 domains operated by scammers, and recovered more than $119 million while investigating more than 1,540 business email compromise incidents. Secret Service-led cases included the identification of a cryptocurrency investment conspiracy operated from scam centers in Cambodia that targeted at least 174 U.S. victims. In October, a Chinese national was extradited from the Netherlands and arraigned in the Central District of California for his alleged role in that conspiracy.

    “While we are encouraged by the progress made to date, our investigators continue to lead dozens of cases involving transnational criminal networks targeting the American people,” remarked U.S. Secret Service Director Sean Curran. “Today’s announcement demonstrates that scammers operating anywhere in the world can be identified and brought to justice. The Secret Service remains committed to its founding mission of investigating financial crimes and will continue to work with law enforcement partners in the United States and around the world to dismantle and disrupt these criminal networks.”.

    Sources indicate that during the surge period, USPIS supported cases against dozens of defendants, including those who perpetrated jury duty imposter schemes described above, lottery and sweepstakes fraud, inheritance fraud, and fraud against Spanish-speaking Americans. Several of these cases involved prosecutions of list brokers who knowingly provided the names of elderly Americans to fraudsters operating abroad. USPIS also seized three internet domains linked to jury duty imposter schemes perpetrated by Georgia prison inmates. Traffic to all three web addresses was redirected to official government servers displaying a public seizure banner. This coordinated takedown effectively dismantled the operators’ digital infrastructure and prevented further public victimization. USPIS also partnered with the Justice Department to mail out over 4,800 unlicensed money transmitter letters since March, which has had an incredible impact on the rates of reducing recidivism for “money mules.”.

    “Behind every scam is a person whose financial security, trust, and peace of mind have been threatened,” stated Chief Inspector Gary Barksdale. “The Postal Inspection Service brings investigative expertise, nationwide reach, and a longstanding commitment to protecting consumers to this effort. Together with the Department of Justice and our partners, the USPIS is working to disrupt these criminal networks, pursue accountability, and prevent others from becoming victims.”.

    During the surge period, the FTC filed 16 actions challenging deceptive earnings claims, unfair payment processing practices, tech support scams, debt relief schemes, unauthorized billing practices, misleading claims about health products, health insurance frauds, government and business impersonations, and deceptive claims about sextortion assistance services. The FTC sent warning letters to a dozen websites advising them of their obligations to comply with the TAKE IT DOWN Act and to 25 companies that market or generate sales leads for healthcare aims, putting them on notice about deceptive or unfair claims that likely violate laws enforced by the FTC. The FTC has continued to work with domain registrars and others to take down social media pages and 19 websites impersonating the FTC or FTC officials. Since April 2026, the FTC has connected more than 365 callers to the Justice Department’s National Elder Fraud Hotline and provided the hotline number to more than 7,100 online filers.

    “The FTC has been on the front lines of tackling fraud for more than a century,” said FTC Chairman and Anti-Fraud Task Force Vice Chairman Andrew N. Ferguson. “Thanks to President Trump’s comprehensive, government-wide approach to stopping fraud, the Trump FTC has returned almost $3 billion to American consumers who have been harmed by fraud and deception. The Trump Administration’s message to the bad actors who lie, cheat and steal to defraud Americans out of their hard-earned money is clear: you are living on borrowed time. The FTC is proud to work alongside its federal partners to protect Americans from scammers, whether the crooks are here at home or abroad.”.

    Securities and Exchange Commission.

    In a recent development, since March 2026, the SEC has filed enforcement actions against 39 entities for allegedly filing false Forms ADV to create the appearance of legitimate U.S. investment advisers and lure retail investors and charged multiple entities with fraud in connection with so-called investment confidence scams that feigned SEC compliance while misappropriating more than $15 million from investors through online platforms. In the last year, the SEC also charged three purported crypto asset trading platforms and four investment clubs with allegedly defrauding retail investors of more than $14 million through an online investment-confidence scam. The SEC charged BG Wealth Sharing Ltd and DSJ Exchange Pty Ltd with an alleged investment fraud scheme that raised more than $130 million from tens of thousands of retail investors across the U.S. and abroad. The SEC has issued investor alerts warning investors that fraudsters may use social media platforms and messaging apps or claim to be officially registered with the SEC to lure investors into scams. The SEC also encourages investors to visit Investor.gov to verify the background of individuals offering investment opportunities.

    In a recent development, “Advances in technology have lowered the barriers to entry for fraudsters, making it easier to reach potential victims and making fraudulent schemes appear more legitimate,” said David Woodcock, Director of the SEC's Division of Enforcement. “The technology may be upcoming, but the frauds are familiar. We will continue working with our law enforcement partners to target these schemes and hold those responsible accountable.”.

    Federal Communications Commission.

    Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 19, the FCC approved a latest rule to allow federal and state prisons and jails to use jamming technology to block calls from illegal contraband cell phones that can be used to coordinate outside illegal activity, including the jury duty scams described above as well as scams explicitly targeting U.S. veterans. The FCC has also taken concrete actions to target scammers and illegal robocallers. The FCC has stopped nearly 300 million illegal robocalls, saving Americans at least $38 million through enforcement and reforms that led to the blocking of more than 1,400 providers and 296 million illegal robocalls. This includes removing from networks voice providers who unlawfully transmitted illegal scammer calls impersonating government agencies, internet service providers, banks, and major retailers. The FCC has published step-by-step guides that enable consumers to turn on blocking and filtering tools specific to devices and carriers.

    “President Trump has put restoring law and order and ensuring the safety of law-abiding Americans at the top of his agenda and that includes stopping scammers. For years, hundreds of thousands of contraband cellphones have entered our prisons allowing offenders to perpetrate scams on ordinary Americans including veteran Jared Johns who took his life after inmates extorted and threatened him. By allowing jamming in prisons for the first time, we’re taking an aggressive, but responsible approach to eliminate inmates access to contraband phones," mentioned Chairman Carr. “The FCC continues to increase our work to crack down on scammers and protect consumers. We’ve taken extensive measures to strengthen consumers’ ability to revoke consent and stop unwanted calls including empowering consumers with instructions to block scam calls and texts, cutting off voices service providers from our networks after non-compliance and further incentivizing providers to block illegal calls so they never get to your phone in the first place.”.

    An indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.
