    #204565. Industry News: Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2339 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, with arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite.
    • Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.
    • According to recent reports, every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, with arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite. Whether you are a Supreme Court follower who usually shunts criminal law to the side, or an experienced criminal law reader who might enjoy some holiday dinner thoughts for your friends and family, this column seeks to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law – and perhaps show why that can be so interesting. To do so, I will scatter some examples from last term, drawn from my recently published Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Cases booklet. When explaining criminal law to your friends or just opining over Thanksgiving dinner, I’d like to show why your mantra should be “crim law is con law” and vice versa.

    Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.

    According to recent reports, every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship. Even non-lawyers know from film and TV that the prosecution’s high burden for proof in a criminal case is beyond a reasonable doubt. But do they know that this is constitutionally required? And perhaps more interesting, that this standard is nowhere, textually, in that document?

    “[T]he Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged,” wrote Justice William Brennan Jr. for the Winship court. If only all Supreme Court decisions had such clear and succinct rule statements.

    According to recent reports, but why is this the rule? It is not found either in the body of the Constitution or in the Bill of Rights, which was adopted soon after the Constitution and focused largely on criminal law protections. Winship‘s answer: because that standard “dates back at least from our early years as a Nation,” “[i]t is now accepted in common law jurisdictions,” it is expressed “in many opinions of this Court,” and it has “long been assumed” to be “constitutionally required.” Thus history, tradition, and precedent support it. Perhaps most fundamentally, a high standard of proof, harder to satisfy than in civil law cases, is essential to fundamental fairness for the public as well as individuals charged with crimes. It is “indispensable to command the respect and confidence of the community” as well as “every individual” exposed to imprisonment. Or, as Justice John Harlan II wrote in an influential concurrence, this standard is “bottomed on a fundamental value determination of our society that it is far worse to convict an innocent man than to let a guilty man go free.”.

    According to recent reports, thus, a fundamental premise of criminal law, Winship, is constitutional law too. Moreover, and just by the way, Winship demonstrates that the “incorporation” theory of the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause (that is, applying the Bill of Rights to the states) is not limited to concepts stated expressly in the Bill of Rights itself – as “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” is not. Critics of non-textual constitutional rights – like privacy, a right to travel, a right to refuse medical treatment (like mask wearing?), or even a right to terminate a pregnancy – must confront the application of their literalist theory to proof beyond a reasonable doubt, too. For this reason, I also teach Winship in every constitutional law class.

    There are almost no crimes mentioned in the Constitution.

    This sometimes surprises 1L students (and others). But the goal of the Constitution was to (re)describe a system of government, and form “a more perfect Union” after the prior Articles of Confederation had proved unsatisfactory. It was not to write a criminal code. The states were then (and still are) the primary forum for criminal law.

    Recent findings suggest that so the Constitution defines only one crime, treason (in Article III, section 3). It mentions a few others, like “Bribery” (in Article II, section 4) and “Breach of the Peace” with a general reference to “Felony” (in Article I, section 6). And of course the Impeachment Clause (Article II section 4) mentions “high Crimes and Misdemeanors,” without definition. Again, states were expected to take care of the substantive definition and application of virtually all criminal law. (However, as I explained some years ago, the First Congress in 1790 did enact over two dozen federal crimes.).

    Yet a large focus of the Bill of Rights is criminal procedure.

    Three years after the Constitution was drafted, the Bill of Rights focused on criminal law rights in at least four proposed amendments (the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth). I won’t list the multitude of rights captured there, but they form the bulk of all criminal procedure law school classes today. The right to be free from unreasonable governmental searches and compelled self-incrimination, and the rights to counsel, jury trials, and no cruel and unusual punishments – and much more – are all embodied in the Bill of Rights.

    Sources indicate that one example from last term: in Villareal v. Texas, the court had to interpret the Sixth Amendment right to “Assistance of Counsel” to decide (unanimously) that a criminal trial judge can order that the defendant not discuss their ongoing testimony with their attorney during an overnight recess.

    In a recent development, why was the Bill of Rights so focused on criminal procedure rights? It’s a fun question to ask students, or at the Thanksgiving table if things get slow. Sooner or later someone gives the soundbite answer: “because most of the constitution’s framers were crooks.” They were certainly guilty of treason – then and still today a capital (that is, death penalty) offense, as well as other crimes (violence, destruction of property, incitement, and more). Had the revolutionary Framers been captured by the government (the British) they likely would have been hung. Instead, during the course of the revolution, numbers had been tried in absentia, found guilty by officials (not juries), and had their houses searched and occupied by troops. Cruel and unusual torture had been inflicted on some captured compatriots. When constitutional ratifying conventions demanded a bill of rights, protections from unfair criminal processes were therefore topmost on the minds of many drafters (if not perhaps “the People” at the time).

    In a recent development, (Another aside: ask your lawyer friends to compare the content of civil procedure versus criminal procedure classes today. The latter full-semester course is almost entirely constitutional law – I used to call my own crim pro class “Con Law Three.” By contrast, civil procedure classes, also a full semester, focus largely on the nitty-gritty details of federal rules, only occasionally wandering into statutes or the Constitution.).

    According to recent reports, in addition to the four explicitly criminal-focused amendments, you might then add general constitutional ideas that are bound to capture some criminal law cases: the First, Second, Third, and Ninth Amendments. The First Amendment’s direction, that “Congress shall make no law” regarding (“respecting”) or abridging freedoms of religion, speech, and the press, is a constitutional law command against criminal laws as well as civil. So too is a protection of a right to keep and bear arms, and to not have government troops quartered in “any” house (not just your own).

    And then consider the “great generalities” of the Constitution.

    In his 1921 Storrs Lectures at Yale Law School (subsequently published as “The Nature of the Judicial Process”), future Supreme Court Justice (and then New York Court of Appeals Judge) Benjamin Cardozo discussed “the great generalities of the Constitution.” Among these, the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the 14th Amendment are huge sources of criminal law doctrine. Just last term, for example, the procedural steps required to apply the Equal Protection Clause against racial (and other) bias in jury selection, and the idea that due process and judicial integrity requires a “miscarriage of justice” exception to guilty plea waivers, received focused Supreme Court attention (in Pitchford v. Cain and Hunter v. United States, respectively).

    Criminal law cases focused on the meaning and application of these broad constitutional requirements arise regularly almost every Supreme Court term. Indeed, as I advise my students every year (again I aspire to teach with a smile, not didactic cynicism): no matter what arguments you make on the defense side of a criminal case, always add the words “and in violation of due process” to preserve at least a thread of a constitutional argument that you may not even perceive at the moment.

    In addition to equal protection and due process, I (and others) would add the Ninth Amendment, which speaks of unspecified “rights … retained by the people.” Justices have sometimes suggested that the Ninth and Tenth Amendments state nothing but “truism[s],” while other Supreme Court decisions have relied (at least in part) on the Ninth. For some, invocation of the Ninth Amendment may provoke if not laughter (it having been referred to by one academic as a “constitutional jester”), then a distinctly conservative or “originalist” rejection. Yet other conservative scholars such as John Yoo and Calvin Massey (my late former colleague) have written expansively about it. As Randy Barnett has argued, the Ninth Amendment “means what it says,” and is “a significant guarantee of individual liberty.” If that is so, then it is (or could be) another source of criminal law protection for criminal defendants.

    For example, Griswold v. Connecticut recognized a constitutional right to privacy in the criminal law context, resting in part (and almost entirely for three justices) on the Ninth Amendment. Less controversially, perhaps, Chief Justice Warren Burger later invoked the amendment in the 1980 case of Richmond Newspapers v. Virginia to support an “unarticulated” constitutional right for the public (and the press) to attend criminal trials. And in 2000, even Justice Antonin Scalia agreed (in a solo dissent to Troxel v. Granville, a non-criminal case) that the Ninth Amendment recognizes unenumerated rights. When you tell your Thanksgiving dinner companions that criminal law is constitutional law, don’t forget the Ninth Amendment.

    So criminal law is, very often, constitutional law.

    Thus it should be unsurprising (as detailed in my Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Law booklet) that 22 of the court’s merits decisions last term that address criminal law involved elements of constitutional law (17 fully argued cases plus five summary (unargued) decisions). That’s a substantial percentage of the court’s entire merits opinions docket, roughly a quarter or more.

    Statutory criminal law cases also often involve constitutional law.

    According to recent reports, by now I hope that you are persuaded: criminal law is (often) constitutional law. “But wait – there’s more!” When you combine the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause with the oft-cited judicial doctrine of constitutional avoidance, criminal cases requiring statutory interpretation also fall into this category. That is, these are criminal law cases that involve consideration of constitutional law. Advocates in statutory cases often raise potential constitutional objections to a criminal statute or to its application in their case, or they may raise constitutional law ideas in favor of their preferred interpretation. In addition, an understanding of constitutional doctrine can be necessary to properly evaluate the merits of a statutory claim. The bottom line is that, in many statutory criminal cases, explication or consideration of constitutional law is necessary or helpful to explain the result.

    Just a few examples from last term: In Barrett v. United States, the court had to mine the details of double jeopardy doctrine to agree, unanimously, that a statute could be interpreted as not permitting two convictions for a single act, thereby avoiding a constitutional problem. In Olivier v. City of Brandon, the court had to examine Olivier’s constitutional claims in order to decide whether the federal civil rights statutes were a proper vehicle for him to sue under. And in Whitton v. Dixon, the court had to briefly explain the constitutional Giglio doctrine, regarding a prosecutor’s failure to disclose exculpatory impeachment information, to reverse an application of the federal habeas corpus statue.

    Sources indicate that immigration cases also often require constitutional law, either to dispose of the merits or to resolve statutory issues in them. Last term’s birthright citizenship case, Trump v. Barbara, is the most obvious example. Because immigration and criminal law cases are often intertwined – consider recent ICE arrests, detentions, and criminal violation grounds for removal – I include them in my annual review as well as the purview of this column. And even civil cases that I consider related to criminal law often require consideration of constitutional law concepts. For example, last term’s Hencely v. Fluor Corp., rejecting a claim of government contractor immunity, required consideration of constitutional preemption doctrine.

    In other words, criminal law mixed with constitutional law is everywhere.

    In a recent development, last week, many of us were focused on the details of elections around the country, substantial and small. And next week, after Thanksgiving, will be chock full of criminal law and related Supreme Court oral arguments. So I’ve tried to give you a break today, and provide a few thoughts that are, perhaps, entertaining, or provocative, or at least interesting ways to navigate your mealtime gatherings (rather than focusing on the usual subjects). For some of you, perhaps this column has simply demonstrated what you already considered obvious; or perhaps it has opened interesting linkages in your mind between constitutional law and criminal law. In any case, thanks for reading this far. Next week I hope you are fortunate enough to breathe relaxing breaths, give thanks, and dwell not on legal minutiae but on what really matters.

    Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

    Recommended Citation: Rory Little, Criminal law is constitutional law, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 20, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/criminal-law-is-constitutional-law/.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that jeffrey Moritz has written in the Columbus Dispatch that his father’s $30 million donation to Ohio State University’s law school has inexplicably fallen and has only provided 12 to 15 scholarships each year. (Image from Shutterstock).

    When Michael Moritz donated more than $30 million to Ohio State University’s law school in 2001, he expected that the money would fund four faculty chairs and 30 annual law school scholarships.

    According to recent reports, but despite that agreement, records from the law school renamed after him show that the fund inexplicably fell from $30 million to $21.9 in less than 15 years, his son Jeffrey Mortiz writes in the Columbus Dispatch. Only 12 to 15 scholarships have been provided annually, he adds.

    In the column, Moritz called upon the Ohio legislature to fix this by passing the Endowment Accountability Act, House Bill 751 and Senate Bill 368 by the end of December. The bill states that donors who believe a public university has violated an endowment agreement must first notify the state’s attorney general, who has 180 days to correct course. Donors in Ohio now have no clear way to hold public universities accountable.

    Sources indicate that A former head of Baker & Hostetler’s corporate practice and director of Cardinal Health, Michael Moritz attended Ohio State’s law school on a full-ride scholarship before graduating in 1958. Less than a year after making his donation, Moritz, 68, was killed by a hit-and-run driver in Naples, Florida.

    We’re looking for a contractSenior Project Manager to own the end-to-end delivery of website and digital projects at N4 Studio, from initial scoping through to launch.

    You’ll be responsible for keeping projects moving across design, development and content, making sure timelines, budgets and scope stay on track while keeping both clients and internal teams clear, confident and aligned.

    Sources indicate that this is a senior delivery role. You’ll need to be comfortable managing multiple projects at once, spotting risks before they become problems, navigating changing priorities and making sure the right people have what they need to deliver great work.

    We build exclusively in Webflow, so strong Webflow (or similar) knowledge is important. You don’t need to be a developer, but you do need to understand the platform and how Webflow websites are designed and built so you can successfully scope, plan and manage projects through delivery.

    N4 Studio is a global digital agency of around 60 people, specialising in Webflow design, development, and growth.     It has been revealed that we operate fully remote, with clients and teammates across New Zealand, Australia, North America, the UK and EU.     #204554. The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2221 w)

    The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that around 2 p.m.
    • Industry observers note that the station later said it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl.
    • Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that around 2 p.m. on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio. Fresh York’s WBAI, a nonprofit radio station, was airing a program on modern attitudes toward language. Near the end, the station played George Carlin’s “Filthy Words” routine, which begins with the comedian saying he’d been thinking about “the words you couldn’t say on the public airwaves; the ones you definitely wouldn’t say, ever.” He went on to repeat those words several times, contrasting them with words like “bastards,” “hell,” and “damn,” which were mostly acceptable, and showing how even some of his list of seven were perfectly fine in other contexts. His point was to show the absurdity of profanity.

    Industry observers note that the station later said it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl. Carlin, the station explained, was doing more than “mouthing obscenities.” He was “using words to satirize as harmless and essentially silly our attitudes towards those words.”.

    Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense. But about a month later, John Douglas complained to the Federal Communications Commission about the transmission which he stated was “garbage” and had been broadcast in the presence of his “young son.” He was the only listener to do so. A member of Morality in Media who frequently listened to the station to “see how far” they’d go, Douglas later acknowledged that he had laughed out loud at the bit but “did not appreciate WBIA’s ‘smart-alecky’ on-air provocations.”.

    Industry observers note that the previous year, Carlin had been arrested after performing an earlier version of the same routine, but a judge threw out the charge. This time, the FCC found the broadcast “indecent,” and put its order in the station’s license file.

    That order ended up before the Supreme Court.

    According to recent reports, early in its order, the FCC acknowledged that Congress had forbade it from censoring broadcasts. But Congress had also prohibited the broadcast of “obscene, indecent, or profane” language, and the Commission thought Carlin’s broadcast fit the bill. In the FCC’s view, the ban on “indecent” language covered not just obscenity, but also patently offensive language when there was a reasonable risk of children listening. Late at night, when children were unlikely to be listening, the same material might be okay if it appeared in a work of serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.

    Two commissioners thought even that was too permissive. Charlotte Reid believed “this language to be totally inappropriate for broadcast at anytime” and thought the commission’s standard did “not go far enough.” Commissioner James Quello took much the same view. “Garbage is garbage,” he wrote, whether children were listening or not.

    The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, however, set aside the order in a 2-1 vote, with one judge believing it violated the statutory ban on censorship and the other saying it violated the First Amendment. The FCC appealed to the Supreme Court.

    In a recent development, at oral argument, which was held in April of 1978, several justices made their distaste for Carlin’s bit plain. When Pacifica’s lawyer stressed that the station had warned listeners beforehand and aired the monologue as part of an educational program about language, Chief Justice Warren Burger incredulously asked, “This is educational in your view?” And when counsel defended the material’s artistic value, Justice Thurgood Marshall responded, “Well, I’m not an expert, but if that’s artistic, deliver me.” Justice William Rehnquist, for his part, tested the limits of Pacifica’s position with a hypothetical involving a single four-letter word repeated for an hour. Would the FCC be powerless to prohibit that? Justice John Paul Stevens, however, seemed troubled by the potential reach of the FCC’s position, given that the prohibition on indecency could be enforced through criminal law.

    In a recent development, one striking exchange concerned the Justice Department’s position to argue separately, and more narrowly, than the FCC. The solicitor general’s office urged that the First Amendment prevented the government from barring particular words outright for a substantial part of the day without regard to context, even if the FCC could constitutionally regulate “indecency” to some extent. Rehnquist sharply asked why the Justice Department was arguing against the FCC, what interest it had in seeking a narrow construction of an act of Congress, and whether the solicitor general, as the government’s lawyer, could ever argue that an act of Congress was unconstitutional.

    It has been revealed that justice Lewis Powell also pressed the DOJ on the reasons behind its departure from the FCC, noting that the DOJ had supported the FCC in the court below. “That is true, and that is an embarrassment to us,” Deputy Solicitor General Louis Claiborne acknowledged, suggesting it was because the matter had been handled there by the Antitrust Division rather than the Criminal Division. Another explanation, which he did not mention, was that the administration had changed.

    The court ultimately ruled 5-4 that the FCC could constitutionally treat this broadcast as “indecent” under the governing statute, and that the government could constitutionally prohibit indecency even though it fell short of legal obscenity. Stevens wrote for Burger, Justice Harry Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist, having apparently struggled with the case and flip-flopped before settling against Pacifica. The Commission had treated the piece as a nuisance, and, as the court had observed in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., a nuisance could be as simple as “a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard.” He concluded that “when the Commission finds that a pig has entered the parlor, the exercise of its regulatory power does not depend on proof that the pig is obscene.” Though the holding expanded the government’s power to regulate speech, Stevens emphasized broadcasting’s pervasive presence in the home and its accessibility to children, the fact the piece was broadcast during the daytime, and the narrowness of the holding. He did not address late night broadcasts or the “occasional expletive.”.

    Recent findings suggest that stevens had only three votes for some parts of his opinion. Powell, joined by Blackmun, wrote separately to object to Stevens’ suggestion that the level of protection that speech receives should depend on a judge’s perception of that speech’s value. For them, the combination of repeated, patently offensive language, an afternoon broadcast, and children’s ready access was enough to resolve the case. Powell also addressed the concern that the decision could end up “reduc[ing] the adult population . . . to [hearing] only what is fit for children”: adults could buy tapes or hear the same words at theaters.

    It has been revealed that justice Potter Stewart dissented, joined by Justices William Brennan, Byron White, and Marshall. Stewart would have resolved the case on statutory grounds. He read “indecent” to reach only obscene material, and everyone agreed that Carlin’s monologue fell outside that category. His opinion recalled his concurrence in Jacobellis v. Ohio, where he voted to overturn an obscenity conviction for showing a French film with an explicit love scene. Stewart understood obscenity narrowly, but declined to define it, famously observing in that case, “I know it when I see it, and the motion picture involved in this case is not that.”.

    Brennan wrote a separate dissent, joined by Marshall, that went further. He agreed with Stewart on the statute and said he would ordinarily refrain from addressing the constitutional question, but he found “the Court’s misapplication of fundamental First Amendment principles so patent, and its attempt to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people so misguided,” that he was “unable to remain silent.”.

    Brennan disputed the analogy between a radio broadcast and an intrusion into the home. Listeners voluntarily turn on the radio, and they can voluntarily turn it off. In perhaps his sharpest passage, he wrote:.

    Brennan also questioned the majority’s reliance on protecting children. He read the court’s precedents as allowing the government to shield children from material that was obscene as to them. In his view, Carlin’s routine fell outside that category. Keeping it off the radio during the afternoon cut off access for adults as well as children. And while the majority had invoked parents’ right to raise their children as they saw fit, Brennan thought the FCC had somewhat ironically made the choice for them.

    Finally, he remained unconvinced that the court’s reasoning would reach only cases like Carlin’s. Among the things it could sweep in were “literary works, novels, poems, and plays by the likes of Shakespeare, Joyce, Hemingway, Ben Jonson, Henry Fielding, Robert Burns, and Chaucer,” “a good deal of political speech, such as the Nixon tapes,” and even portions of the Bible. In his view, the public, and not the court, should have the power to weed out “worthless and offensive” speech in a marketplace “unsullied by the censor’s hand.”.

    Recent findings suggest that brennan and Marshall had joined together in another Supreme Court opinion involving the F-word. In Cohen v. California, they joined Justice John Harlan II’s opinion protecting the right to wear a jacket emblazoned with “Fuck the Draft.” Stewart joined it too (not surprisingly, Burger and Blackmun dissented). Brennan brought Cohen straight into his Pacifica dissent; as he made clear, changing the words can change what the speaker communicates, something that applies especially well to Carlin because the taboo words were themselves the subject of the routine. And Brennan thought telling listeners to buy a record or pay to see Carlin live missed what it meant to hear the routine on the radio.

    Sources indicate that in closing, Brennan wrote that the majority had only “confirm[ed] Carlin’s prescience as a social commentator.” (It was interesting that Marshall, who sounded distinctly unimpressed by the claim of artistic merit at oral argument, joined him, perhaps especially here.) As Brennan pointed out, Carlin had made fun of the rules about which words you could say on the air, and the court had exemplified the very attitude he was satirizing. To top it all off: Appended to the opinion is the transcript of Carlin’s routine, giving his “indecent” words a permanent home in the U.S. Reports.

    Recent findings suggest that at the 2002 Billboard Music Awards on Fox, Cher dispatched the critics who’d spent decades predicting her downfall with “So f*** ’em.” At the 2003 awards, Nicole Richie asked whether anyone had tried getting cow manure out of a Prada purse, then used the F-word to describe how hard it was. The next year, after Bono called U2’s Golden Globe win “really, really f***ing brilliant,” the FCC announced that even a single expletive could be indecent, and it later applied that approach to the two earlier Fox broadcasts.

    It has been revealed that in 2009, the Supreme Court took up the dispute in FCC v. Fox Television Stations. Writing for a 5-4 majority, Justice Antonin Scalia held that the FCC had adequately explained its change in policy under the Administrative Procedure Act, leaving the First Amendment question open. Justice Clarence Thomas joined the majority but wrote separately to question Pacifica’s holding. On remand, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit struck down the policy as unconstitutionally vague.

    Recent findings suggest that the case returned to the Supreme Court in 2012 and all eight participating justices agreed on the result (Justice Sonia Sotomayor recused herself). Justice Anthony Kennedy’s opinion held that the FCC had failed to give Fox fair notice that fleeting expletives could trigger an indecency finding, but once again left both Pacifica and the First Amendment question open. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote separately to say that Pacifica was wrong from the start and deserved reconsideration. But while the court has had several cases involving curse words since, it has yet to take up the question directly.

    In 2004, the FCC dismissed complaints related to the airing of Saving Private Ryan on the basis that the film’s curse words helped convey the soldiers’ experience. But just two years later, it slapped a station with $15,000 in fines for airing a Martin Scorsese documentary about Blues music that contained profanity. In 2020, the FCC received over 1,300 complaints about Jennifer Lopez and Shakira’s halftime show, though it never took any action against the network. And in February 2026, FCC requested transcripts of Bad Bunny’s Superbowl halftime performance before ultimately finding no violation.

    Half a century after Carlin’s seven dirty words, the FCC’s continued and seemingly arbitrary application of its indecency laws indicates the prescience of Brennan’s dissent and the need to finally answer the question of whether the Constitution prohibits the “dominant culture” from trying to force “groups who do not share its mores to conform to its way of acting, thinking, and speaking.”.

    Anastasia Boden is a Senior Attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, where she brings civil rights lawsuits that advance the Constitution’s promises of equality and economic opportunity.

    Recommended Citation: Anastasia Boden, The Supreme Court and profanity, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 23, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-supreme-court-and-profanity/.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The king tides caused massive waves, but little more than minor flooding.

    (CN) âÂ Several beaches along the coast of Southern California saw record high tides Wednesday, thanks to the convergence of three factors: the astronomical event known as “king tides,” the “El NiÃ±o” climate cycle, and global warming.

    It has been revealed that preliminary data measured high tide at the Los Angeles Harbor, in the San Pedro neighborhood, at 8.19 feet, tying the previous record of about a month ago, with records going all the way back to 1923. La Jolla and Santa Barbara had all-time record high tides, though the data for Santa Barbara only goes as far back as 1990.

    State and local officials, including Governor Gavin Newsom, had warned extensive flooding could disrupt travel intends and flood coastal communities. Those fears appear not to have been fully realized.

    Todd Hall, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service’s Los Angeles office in Oxnard, said two factors prevented the tides from being worse: Storm surge in Northern California petered out, and the high tide and large swells happened independently.

    Sources indicate that “There is some reprieve, because the high tide this morning, surf and swell coming up into tonight,” Hall mentioned. “Things would be much worse if we had high surf arriving at the same time we had high tide.”.

    Some areas did see minor flooding. Streets were underwater in the low-lying neighborhood of Sunset Beach in Huntington Beach this morning. Meanwhile, in the Bay Area, water from San Francisco Bay spilled onto the Embarcadero, and in Pacifica massive waves destroyed a section of the municipal pier. Santa Cruz County and Marin County both issued evacuation warnings for homes along the coast, though the latter has already been lifted.

    Warnings and advisories remain in place up and down the coast, but so far, the king tides have been less destructive than feared.

    “It is a relief, that things weren’t worse,” stated Febe Rothenberg, meteorologist at the National Weather Service in San Francisco. Still, she warned: “Pretty please, avoid the beach.”.

    According to recent reports, king tides, also called perigean spring tides, are predictable astronomical events that occur when a fresh or full moon lines up with both the sun and Earth. The gravitational pull of the three bodies combine and cause exceptionally high tides. The next king tide will be a month from now, on Christmas Eve, when tides could be even higher if a storm hits.

    This year’s especially strong El NiÃ±o means unusually warm surface waters in the Pacific Ocean, with higher-than-average tides, larger waves and more frequent storms.

    Scientists predict tides will be higher and higher because of global warming, which has melted glaciers and caused ocean levels to rise 3-4 inches in the last 30 years.

    According to recent reports, U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan granted the news agencyâs motion for a preliminary injunction to halt the ongoing license renewal process and denied the Justice Departmentâs motion to dismiss the case on jurisdictional grounds.

    According to recent reports, âThis is not a close case,â the Joe Biden appointee wrote inÂ her 45-page opinion. âNo one doubts that the commission may enforce the law in the manner it sees fit. But in doing so, defendants may not retaliate against or punish plaintiffs or other broadcast license holders for disfavored speech.â.

    âPlaintiffs have a weighty interest in âvindicating the[ir] right to be free of retaliation for [their] protected speech. And âthere is always a strong public interest in the exercise of free speech rights otherwise abridged by an unconstitutionalâ government action.â.

    AliKhan rejected the governmentâs argument that the license renewal was inherently tied to an initial March 2025 anti-discrimination probe into Disneyâs hiring practices â part of the Justice Departmentâs ongoing campaign to roll back diversity, equity and inclusion practices â and the companyâs refusal to provide requested documents.

    The FCCâs license review of ABC News and eight of its regional affiliates â the stationâs licenses were set to expire between December 2028 and August 2031 â is the first use of the process in nearly 60 years, Wilkinson said.     It has been revealed that the Disney CompanyÂ sued the Trump administration on Aug. 18, seeking an order blocking the FCC from issuing a hearing designation order, where the company anticipated its renewal applications or licenses could be revoked.

    The tech giant highlighted how the âJimmy Kimmel Live!â late show was temporarily suspended last year following the comedianâs comments regarding the assassination of right-wing debater Charlie Kirk suggesting the GOP sought to âscore political pointsâ off his death.

    Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (273 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that in September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion.
    • Since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view.
    • Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    Sources indicate that in September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion. In her acceptance speech, Jackson discussed Brennan’s role as the Supreme Court became more conservative, noting that he “believed that even his dissents could make a difference and remind the nation that the pursuit of equal justice under law is an ongoing effort.” Jackson indicated that she agreed with that idea, telling the audience that she saw “dissent[s] as more than just a disagreement with the outcome of a case, I see them as an expression of faith in the future and a demonstration of hope.” As she put it, “However desolate the moment feels, we who write for a future age have hope that the noble and collective work of bending the long arc of the law toward justice will continue.”.

    Since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view. Although she has been consistently part of the court’s liberal bloc, even among the three Democratic appointees she has forged a unique role. As her invocation of Brennan suggests, it often appears that her goal is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision and to speak to the public directly – even if she does so without the support of her fellow liberals.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    Latest Update: The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1813 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.
    • Sources indicate that on November 10, The New York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v.
    • According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

    Sources indicate that on November 10, The New York Times published an article suggesting that a major piece of the Supreme Court’s Second Amendment jurisprudence is premised on a misquote by the late Justice Antonin Scalia in his 2008 majority opinion in D.C v. Heller, in which the court held that there was an individual right to possess firearms. The essence of the piece is that Scalia used the phrase “dangerous and unusual” to describe those weapons not protected by the right to keep and bear arms, attributing this terminology primarily (or perhaps solely) to the 18th century British jurist William Blackstone. Yet Blackstone’s writings instead use the phrase “dangerous or unusual.”.

    According to the Times piece, “[t]he consequences of Justice Scalia’s use of ‘and’ rather than ‘or’ have been profound”: “Since all guns are dangerous, courts have had to focus instead on determining whether a type of firearm is unusual, often parsing marketing data and consumer surveys to gauge a weapon’s popularity.” Presumably, if Scalia had used the phrase “dangerous or unusual,” it would be easier for legislatures to ban even certain commonly owned firearms because dangerousness alone would be sufficient to bring a category of weapons outside the amendment’s protective sphere.

    It has been revealed that the Times story has reverberated promptly, with strong backlash from conservative lawyers and scholars. Such disagreements have focused largely on the specific citation Scalia used. Law professor Jonathan Adler, for example, has argued that the citation to Blackstone was one among many, and additional sources that Scalia cited used the “and” formulation. Others have responded that Scalia was anything but sloppy, which would be especially true when it came to such an influential and vital source.

    Both sides, though, seem to be burying the lede. In my view, this is a story not about historical errors or the nuances of legal citation. Rather, it is about how judicial dicta that was never intended to lay down broad, permanent rules has taken on a life of its own, and how other justices on the Supreme Court subsequently canonized Scalia’s stray language by turning it into a “test” that would govern any number of future cases – when it’s not at all clear Scalia ever contemplated this or would have endorsed any such thing.

    As most law students and lawyers are well aware, the holding-dicta distinction is deeply rooted in American jurisprudence: generally speaking, the holding is the analysis necessary to resolve the actual case before the court, and everything else in an opinion is dicta (this comes from the Latin phrase “obiter dictum,” or “stated in passing”). Fundamental to that distinction is that dicta, while it may be persuasive, is not precedential. As Chief Justice John Marshall wrote in 1821, the reason for not deferring blindly to dicta is “obvious”:.

    The late Judge Richard Posner once similarly emphasized the risk that dicta “can be misleading if carelessly lifted from the case-specific contexts in which they were originally uttered … That is why courts in assessing the binding effect of previous decisions distinguish between the dicta, which are the inessential parts of the opinion, and the holding.” Circuits vary in their approach to Supreme Court dicta, generally deferring more heavily to such language when they find it thoroughly considered or supported, but the court is, of course, never bound by its own dicta.

    In fact, Scalia himself was no fan of relying heavily on dicta from prior Supreme Court decisions. In a 1993 opinion, he criticized a group of dissenting justices by noting that their position found “support, if at all, only in the dicta of this Court’s opinions.” This was, in Scalia’s view, as good as no support at all. Indeed, Scalia rejected reliance on “drive-by … rulings” not fully considered by the issuing court, even if not purely dicta. In his 2015 decision for the court in Kerry v. Din, Scalia excoriated a proposition advanced in a dissenting opinion as resting solely on “dictum in a footnote” and then observed that “[t]he footnoted dictum that Justice Breyer proposes to elevate to constitutional law is a dangerous doctrine.” He further joined opinions that rejected prior dicta as unprincipled, especially when greater investigation revealed reasons for caution.

    Scalia’s position was nuanced – for example, he once joined a dissent by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg that endorsed reliance on certain dictum as persuasive – yet a cautious approach to dicta is consistent with his broader judicial philosophy as well. He was at times willing to jettison even precedential decisions squarely applicable to the case at hand when those decisions were contrary to original public meaning. Unconsidered dicta, presumably, would then be far lower in the pecking order.

    Sources indicate that returning to Heller and the phrase at problem, it’s hard to argue that the “dangerous and unusual” passage from Heller is anything but dicta. The issue in Heller was whether a Washington, D.C. ordinance “generally prohibit[ing] the possession of handguns” violated the Second Amendment, or if there was an individual right to keep arms for one’s self-defense. Scalia’s majority opinion answered in the affirmative, as “the American people have considered the handgun to be the quintessential self-defense weapon.” D.C. never argued that handguns were entirely exempt from protection because they were especially dangerous. The question of dangerous and/or unusual weapons was not at issue in the case; accordingly, it wasn’t thoroughly investigated through the adversarial process.

    Rather, after canvassing the historical evidence and concluding it supported an individual-rights view of the Second Amendment, Scalia turned to the nature of the right he had just explicated. In three short paragraphs not necessary to the holding, he explained why the amendment did not authorize gun keeping-and-carrying by anyone in any circumstance; rather history revealed limitations on the right, such as “the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’”.

    Whatever the purpose of this section – Justice John Paul Stevens later suggested the language was proposed by Justice Anthony Kennedy (the crucial fifth vote in Heller) in exchange for joining the majority – it was far from necessary to resolve the case at hand.

    In a recent development, so how did such dicta become relevant? In the 2016 case Caetano v. Massachusetts, decided after Scalia had passed away, the justices unanimously overturned a Massachusetts Supreme Court decision upholding that state’s ban on stun guns in a criminal prosecution of a woman who used this weapon to defend herself from an abusive ex-boyfriend. Justice Samuel Alito issued a concurring opinion (joined by Justice Clarence Thomas) that performed an interesting maneuver. Seizing on the fact that the per curiam opinion in that case referenced Scalia’s “dangerous and unusual” formulation, Alito turned Scalia’s language into a doctrinal test: “As the per curiam opinion recognizes, this is a conjunctive test: A weapon may not be banned unless it is both dangerous and unusual.” But the per curiam had done no such thing; rather, that opinion simply cited the passage in Heller as referring to one limitation on the right to keep and bear arms. And the per curiam mentioned that the lower court in that case had faltered by concluding that any weapon not in common use in 1791 was per se unusual, not by failing to use a conjunctive test.

    (Ironically, Alito has his own well-publicized objections to giving past Supreme Court dicta undue veneration – his opinion for the court in Dobbs heavily suggested that Roe’s viability framework was entitled to less weight in the stare decisis analysis because it was initially mere dicta, “the Court’s own brainchild [for which n]either party advocated.”).

    In a recent development, from there, the “dangerous and unusual” language took on a life of its own. In 2022’s New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, in which the court struck down New York’s concealed-carry law, the majority set forth a test for Second Amendment constitutionality privileging historical evidence above all else. At the first step of that test, a court determines whether the conduct at issue is protected by the right to keep and bear arms, which is where the exclusion of dangerous and/or unusual weapons becomes relevant. If the banned weapon is not protected by the Second Amendment (for, say, being “dangerous and unusual”), a constitutional challenge is dead on arrival. If, on the other hand, the plaintiff can show the weapons are protected, then the burden switches to the government to provide historical evidence to support its regulation. (The consequences may be even greater, as some have argued that “usualness” (or “common use”) conclusively establishes not only threshold protection for the weapon but also that any legislative ban is ahistorical and thus unconstitutional.).

    This test has divided the judiciary in recent years. For example, a Massachusetts federal judge evaluating a challenge to that state’s AR-15 ban recognized the apparent disconnect between Heller and Blackstone but nevertheless noted that “the Supreme Court has expressly stated . . .that the relevant tradition is one of regulating ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’” The Massachusetts judge found these weapons were not in “common use,” and, in any event, a historical tradition of responding to technological advances by regulating specific weapons supported the ban. By contrast, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit interpreted Scalia’s language to signal that widespread ownership of AR-15s and large-capacity magazines meant any legislative attempt to ban them was unconstitutional. The “dangerous and unusual” framework has led other judges on a search for ownership statistics and sales data to assess a weapon’s popularity, triggering sharp debate over whether a test that ultimately turns on commonality is even workable.

    This is particularly relevant since the court is presently preparing to hear oral argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, a Second Amendment challenge to state and local bans on AR-15s, on December 2. While the recent attention to Scalia’s citation may trigger discussion at oral argument, most justices are now likely to treat “dangerous and unusual” as an established standard and ownership statistics as definitive proof that AR-15s are not unusual and thus protected. Absent from this, however, will be the fact that this standard did not emerge from any well-reasoned, litigation-tested analysis making it deserve deference in the first place – especially under Scalia’s own approach to judging.

    The debate over Scalia’s Blackstone citation, then, has obscured a more key problem: the Supreme Court’s decision to treat its past dicta as doctrine that can settle the outcome of cases on which the court has never passed.

    Andrew Willinger is an Assistant Professor at Georgia State University College of Law, where he teaches constitutional law and civil procedure.

    Recommended Citation: Andrew Willinger, The Second Amendment and an "unusually dangerous" approach to dicta, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 23, 2026, 10:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-second-amendment-and-an-unusually-dangerous-approach-to-dicta/.

    #204547. Latest Update: Judge doesn’t like your objections? Here are some tips to keep them coming in a meaningful way

    📅 30 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1089 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Judge doesn’t like your objections? Here are some tips to keep them coming in a meaningful way

    📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1089 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Porto gets calls all the time from lawyers or litigants who want to appeal a verdict from a case that went horribly wrong.
    • Industry observers note that sometimes the problem is a bad jury instruction.
    • Porto, who specializes in appellate civil issues, wants to be able to deliver good news, but it’s not always possible, particularly if the attorneys failed to object in proper, timely way.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, juli M. Porto gets calls all the time from lawyers or litigants who want to appeal a verdict from a case that went horribly wrong.

    Industry observers note that sometimes the problem is a bad jury instruction. Sometimes it’s a devastating ruling on key evidence. Sometimes the issue is the judge’s failure to stop opposing counsel from badgering a witness.

    Porto, who specializes in appellate civil issues, wants to be able to deliver good news, but it’s not always possible, particularly if the attorneys failed to object in proper, timely way.

    A principal at Blankingship & Keith in Fairfax, Virginia, Porto warns that typically, no matter how “egregious a trial judge’s error was, if it’s not preserved, it can’t be appealed.”.

    According to recent reports, litigators know they need to preserve the record during court hearings, depositions or trial. And they’re aware that they generally can’t raise an objection for the first time on appeal.

    But still, even the most experienced lawyers hesitate on how much to object and how far to go when advocating for their clients, particularly when judges appear to lose their patience.

    “It can be a delicate balance,” notes J.C. Lore III, director of trial advocacy at Rutgers Law School. “Lawyers don’t want to make the judge angry.”.

    Rule 103 of the Federal Rules of Evidence advises lawyers that objections must be timely and done with specificity.

    While state rules of evidence vary, they tend to follow the same framework as the Uniform Rules of Evidence.

    In addition, the American Bar Association Model Rule of Professional Conduct 1.1 requires lawyers to act competently.

    Tiffany Williams Brewer is chair of the ABA Section of Litigation and a former New Jersey state administrative law judge. She notes a lawyer’s role is to “courteously remind” the judge of the importance of preserving the record.

    “As a former judge, I can relate that judges are often focused on the efficiency of moving the trial forward and may not even realize that they have skipped the opportunity to allow the lawyers to properly put their evidentiary basis on the record,” Brewer claims.

    Most litigators have a war story or two where they felt they were being reasonable and advocating for their client while the judge was being unreasonable and obstructing them. And then there are the extreme cases.

    In a Bexar County, Texas, court in 2024, then-Judge Rosie Speedlin Gonzalez accused an attorney of coaching her client and then pushed back when the attorney objected.

    Gonzalez stated the attorney was “not allowed to be argumentative and argue just for the sake of argument.”.

    As the situation escalated, she ordered the attorney to be handcuffed and placed in the jury box.

    Recent findings suggest that gonzalez was later charged over the incident, then the charges were dropped when she agreed to resign and never again seek reelection. She declined comment to the ABA Journal.

    For the most part, Lore notes, judges know lawyers must make objections and don’t take it personally.

    However, Lore says, when lawyers are using objections as a tactic to disrupt or rattle opposing counsel, judges tend to get angry and push back.

    Amy M. Stewart is a partner at Fisher Phillips in Dallas and chair of the ABA Section of Litigation.

    “No one promised us in law school that making objections would be easy or without anxiety,” Stewart notes.

    Sometimes, dealing with a judge who won’t let counsel make proper objections requires some strategic maneuvering, she adds.

    In one case, her firm hired an appellate lawyer to handle preserving the record during trial. Unfortunately, Stewart says, the judge told the appellate lawyer to “sit down” at critical moments in the trial.

    “Appellate counsel held her own, but the drama was becoming distracting for the jurors,” Stewart notes, so the trial team changed course, and had a male counsel make the objections.

    It has been revealed that “We realized the court never interrupted one of our co-lead counsels on the case,” Stewart says. “We coached him to make these critical objections, and the court would rule.”.

    In a recent development, during his decades of litigation, Jules Epstein has seen all kinds of problems come up during trial with judges who are reasonable and those who are less so. He suggests that if a judge is repeatedly blocking an attorney from making objections, the attorney should approach the judge calmly when the jury is not around.

    “You can say to the judge, ‘I don’t want to violate your protocols, but I have to protect my client. Will you please give me instructions on how you want me to do this?’” says Epstein, director of advocacy programs at Temple University Beasley School of Law.

    If that doesn’t work, he says, a lawyer can file a written pleading or motion to preserve objections, including every single effort made to object in a timely way.

    There’s also the option for an interlocutory appeal, depending on state rules, before a trial has concluded.

    There are times, says Ryan Watstein, that lawyers need to stand up to judges on behalf of their clients, even if that means they “catch a few black eyes” in the process.

    “There are a lot of things culturally built into the practice of law, including a tendency to be intentionally hesitant to push back, particularly on the judiciary,” states Watstein, an Atlanta-based litigator and founding partner of Watstein Terepka.

    In a LinkedIn post in May, Watstein described how he was trying to convince a judge to rein in opposing counsel during discovery. Watstein kept arguing, and the judge yelled, “This is your last chance, Mr. Watstein.”.

    Watstein explains that the courtroom was tense, and his client was uncomfortable. He thought he might get held in contempt.

    According to recent reports, “Every instinct our conservative profession teaches you was telling me to sit down,” Watstein states. “But I didn’t sit down.”.

    Watstein notes he kept talking, despite the judge indicating it was time to stop. He said that he would seek appellate review of the judge’s decision if he didn’t get justice on the issue.

    He ended up convincing the judge to reverse himself.

    Watstein warns against being “overly deferential” when an “injustice is being perpetrated” against your client.

    Sources indicate that “You should always start in way that is respectful and professional, but there are circumstances where you have to push harder,” Watstein says. “The line that lawyers are trained to go up to is not necessarily the appropriate stopping point.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I dedicate my Thanksgiving column each year to the Indian Nation from whom I learned so much, the Tohono Oâodham, with whom I spent six of the best years of my life.

    According to recent reports, I taught English, music and journalism and coached distance runners on the second-largest Indian reservation in the United States. The Oâodham are the only Indian Nation that never was at war with the United States and never were removed from their homelands.

    And I bet youâve never heard of them.

    The reason they never were at daggers drawn with Uncle Sam is that the Oâodham were a sedentary, transhumant agricultural tribe whose perennial enemies were the Apache.

    Transhumant means the quasi-sedentary people moved regularly from one climate zone to another, then returned: highlands in the summer, when itâs so hot on the desert floor, and you can hunt animals on the mountains, then back to the desert when the rains came, to harvest beans and squash.

    In Oâodham itâs called ak chin farming: farming at the mouth of the wash.

    In a recent development, A wash is a dry riverbed. You can see them all over what we call southern Arizona. The only time thereâs water in a wash is right after a monsoon rain. Mark Twain said he fell into a desert river once, âand came up all dusty.â.

    On the year I moved to the rez to teach at Baboquivari High School, I had an average of 43 students in my three English classes, and no desks for students, only the one for me.

    Fortunately, or not, it was the band room, so my students shared music stands to write out my assignments.

    Recent findings suggest that fortunately, or not, the ceiling was falling down, and, stashed in a closet, with a jumble of battered horns â all of our horns were battered â a kindly janitor had left us half a gallon of ceiling plaster. Which I used to patch up the pads on the flutes, saxophones and clarinets.

    Thatâs how it was on the rez when I got there. All but forgotten by Uncle Sam. And in some ways, good riddance to our uncle. But not so good that our uncle wouldnât buy desks for the only public school on the 3-million-acre reservation: twice the size of Delaware.

    Well, you do what you can, and you do what you must.

    Industry observers note that I dug life on the rez. Learning stuff I never knew I didnât know. Tryna pick up the language, and man, thatâs a tough language to learn. About all thatâs stuck with me is, âAyy, jum skug!â.

    Jum skug, as I understand it, means someone is âtrying to act.â Like a substantial shot.

    I tried not to be jum skug. Still try not to.

    According to recent reports, I loved those years on the rez. Those 2,200 days.

    Hereâs another thing I learned. Iâll bet youâve been in this situation: Youâre in a party of mostly white people (mirgan); conversations are bubbling along in a crowded room, then all at once, the room is silent. Two, four seconds pass, then someone states something, probably stupid, just to *break the silence.*People laugh, and the party continues.

    Itâs like the mirgan canât stand silence in a room.

    Iâve been in rooms with Oâodham where that silence continues, and no one feels that itâs necessary to break the silence. When someone finally speaks, itâs because sheâs got something to say â itâs not because she canât stand silence.

    Thereâs nothing wrong with silence.

    Here are some other things I learned on the rez.

    If you donât know what to say, shut up.

    If youâre not sure of what you want to say, shut up.

    If youâre called upon to speak, but donât know what you want to say, or donât know much about the subject: shut up.

    In celebration of Thanksgiving today (Thorâs Day), Iâd like to address all 535 members of Congress, and all of their appointed staffs, all the appointed members of the executive branch, and all the appointed, paid-off, cushy and cowardly members of our Supreme Court: to all of them, and to so many more, in our federal and state houses around the nation, Iâd like to tell yâall what I learned on the rez:.

    If you donât know what youâre talking about, shut the fuck up.

    Europe fast-tracked renewable energy permits after Russian gas supplies fell. A Belgian case tested how much discretion local officials still had under those rules.

    (CN) â The Belgian region Wallonia noted no to two wind turbines near its capital to protect the views, but the EUâs top court ruled Thursday that even scenery could take a back seat to qualifying renewable projects under the blocâs emergency rules.

    Eneco Wind Belgium asked the national Council of State to overturn the Walloon regionâs refusal to let it build and operate the turbines in Andoy, on the outskirts of Namur. The company argued officials had overlooked the priority its project should receive underÂ an emergency EU rule. The Belgian judgesÂ asked the Court of Justice of the European Union how far that rule could go.

    In a recent development, eneco filed for its permit in April 2023, a few months after the EU moved to speed up renewable energy construction. Russiaâs invasion of Ukraine and cuts in Russian gas supplies had sent energy prices soaring. Getting wind and other renewable projects online faster offered a way to replace some of that fuel.

    In a recent development, in Andoy, the prepares called for access roads, a substation and underground cables. A public inquiry drew complaints, and Walloon officials turned down the project that October, citing the areaâs landscape and heritage. Officials reviewing Enecoâs appeal recommended a permit with conditions. The ministers handling the appeal missed the deadline to notify Eneco of a decision, so the refusal stood.

    The EU judgesÂ saidÂ projects recognized as serving an overriding public interest had to get priority even when the competing concern fell outside EU rules on birds, habitats and waterways. Limiting that advantage to those environmental laws, they reasoned, would blunt a measure designed to speed up permitting.

    It has been revealed that for Hendrik Schoukens, a professor of environmental law at Ghent University, the ruling narrowed officialsâ discretion in an area where governments set their own standards. âThis is crucial, since landscape protection is not a harmonized interest by EU law,â he mentioned.

    Sources indicate that officials could still put a competing interest first if they gave reasons specific to the project. The judges pointed to the ruleâs instruction to weigh those interests case by case. âThat provision would be devoid of purpose if the priority of those projects were to arise automatically from the mere recognition of their being of overriding public interest,â the court wrote.

    For projects that needed an exception to EU bird or habitat protections, there was still the question of whether they could go ahead another way. Harm Dotinga, a senior legal adviser on nature protection at BirdLife Netherlands, said a well-supported refusal could still protect biodiversity. He pointed to separate legal requirements, including the need to show there was no satisfactory alternative. âThose may also justify rejection of the project if properly motivated,â he said. Schoukens said it was striking how little attention the Belgian proceedings had paid to alternatives, given that a more sustainable option could still sink a project.

    Industry observers note that whether a project qualified for priority in the first place depended on what stood in its way. Officials could rely on an existing presumption that it served an overriding public interest, including where national law extended that presumption to landscape protection. Where the presumption did not apply or was called into question, the project needed formal recognition.

    Eline Dhaen, a spokesperson for Eneco Belgium, said the company was reviewing the ruling. The Walloon Region did not respond to a request for comment.

    According to recent reports, A permit with conditions, as officials had recommended in Andoy, was another option. The court stated authorities could require developers to limit or make up for environmental damage and, where the law allowed, let some measures follow approval. Where species protection was at stake, the priority rule required conservation measures backed by sufficient funding and land.

    Elisa Cristea, a senior associate specializing in energy and environmental law at Romanian firm Èuca ZbÃ¢rcea & AsociaÈii, welcomed the ruling and saw conditional permits as its most practical point.

    âThis reflects a shift in the approach to permitting: Authorities should consider how competing interests can be accommodated rather than treating them solely as grounds for refusing a project,â she mentioned.

    Industry observers note that cristea remarked the judges left officials more leeway than Advocate General Athanasios Rantos, who had proposed that departures from the priority rule be exceptional and backed by a detailed assessment. She said the ruling could outlast the expired emergency measure if EU lawmakers adoptedÂ a European Commission proposalÂ to restore priority over a wider range of competing interests.

    Thursdayâs ruling is binding and cannot be appealed. Belgiumâs Council of State now has to apply it to the question still open in Andoy: whether Walloniaâs refusal stands.

    (AFP) â A trade deal struck last week between Britain and the EU as part of Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s reset with the bloc contains a termination clause, London confirmed Thursday.

    It comes as the leaders of the right-wing opposition Conservative and Reform UK parties suggested they could seek to scrap the agreements if they defeat Labour at the next general election.

    Burnham has reignited the Brexit wars that dominated political discourse following the narrow victory for the leave campaign during the 2016 referendum by suggesting Britain could apply to rejoin one day.

    The U.K. premier and top EU officials signed three agreements in Brussels on Nov. 20 designed to improve post-Brexit ties in the short-term, kicking decisions on their long-term relationship down the road.

    They include the so-called sanitary and phytosanitary deal, which the British government says could add 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7 billion) to the country’s economy by slashing red tape on food and drink exports.

    It includes a clause meaning that if one party ends the agreement within its first 10 years they would have to pay to rebuild the border checks infrastructure that the deal removes.

    “That termination clause is a standard practice in international treaties, and this one applies equally to both sides, including the EU,” Burnham’s deputy spokesperson told reporters.

    Industry observers note that U.K. officials said an upfront sum for breaking the deal had not been stipulated.

    An EU diplomat told AFP that the reciprocal clause “provides stability for the agreement to deliver its benefits.”.

    Charles Grant, director of the Centre for European Reform think tank, noted it “makes sense” for the EU given the ongoing debate in Britain about its future relations with Brussels.

    “It’s an insurance policy,” he told AFP.

    Friday’s summit also agreed measures linking the two sides’ emissions-trading schemes and allowing young people to study and work across U.K.-EU borders.

    On Thursday, Burnham’s government formally introduced into Parliament the legislation required to implement the trade and electricity agreements.

    It has been revealed that lawmakers will get their first chance to debate them on Dec. 7, with a vote expected to follow, Labour confirmed Thursday.

    The EU Partnership Bill, which the government also refers to as the “Cutting Costs” bill, will almost certainly be approved by the lower House of Commons, where Labour holds a large majority.

    It will see the U.K. align with EU rules for sectors covered by the agreements, something known as dynamic alignment.

    The U.K. government says linking the pair’s carbon markets would create the world’s largest connected carbon market and exempt 6.5 billion pounds’ ($8.1 billion) worth of British exports from EU carbon border taxes.

    London and Brussels have given themselves six more months to reach agreement on reduced university tuition fees for EU students in Britain, a key demand of the bloc.

    Having previously said he would like to see Britain rejoin the EU in his lifetime, Burnham has promised to lay out options that could range from leaving things as they are to entering the customs union or becoming a member again.

    The prime minister has vowed to present his options to the public after a year of “informal brainstorming” with the EU. He mentioned this week that rejoining without a referendum would be “unthinkable.”.

    Several former Conservative prime ministers, including Rishi Sunak, Boris Johnson, Theresa May and David Cameron, have warned against reopening a debate that deeply divided the country.

    Reform leader Nigel Farage noted this week he would “repeal” the reset deal while Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Thursday she “does not support” what Burnham is doing.

    By PETER HUTCHISON Agence France-Presse.
