    Latest Update: What do these Supreme Court plaintiffs have in common?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Hecox, which concerned whether states could bar transgender female athletes from participating in girl’s and women’s sports, Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked Idaho Solicitor General Alan Hurst: “Do you dispute that having a case named after you makes your infamy ...
    • On Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the “Closer Look” section of SCOTUSblog’s daily newsletter to covering the story of some of the most famous plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases.
    • Now 16 installments in, we thought it would be a good time to take a step back and assess what’s been learned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last term in Little v. Hecox, which concerned whether states could bar transgender female athletes from participating in girl’s and women’s sports, Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked Idaho Solicitor General Alan Hurst: “Do you dispute that having a case named after you makes your infamy ... live forever? ... You don't think that Brown and any of the other named plaintiffs that we have in famous cases dr[ew] … attention to those people as people?” Sotomayor asked the question in the context of Hecox requesting that the Supreme Court dismiss the case, citing, in part, “negative public scrutiny ... because of this litigation.”.

    On Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the “Closer Look” section of SCOTUSblog’s daily newsletter to covering the story of some of the most famous plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases.

    Now 16 installments in, we thought it would be a good time to take a step back and assess what’s been learned. In this article, we offer a glimpse at the lives of a baker, a farmer, an executive director at Planned Parenthood, two students, and a leader of the Ku Klux Klan. But besides having interesting (and sometimes disturbing) life stories, what do they all have in common? Each asked the Supreme Court to answer one of the most fundamental questions of all: Where does government power end and personal liberty begin?

    Joseph Lochner: Lochner v. Newly introduced York.

    Let’s start with Joseph Lochner. Lochner immigrated from Bavaria, Germany, to the United States at the age of 20 in 1882, and settled in Utica, Fresh York. He sought employment in the bakery industry; around 1890, he opened his own small, family bakeshop in Utica.

    Recent findings suggest that during this time, efforts emerged across Latest York to regulate the conditions of bakery workers after an article written by Edward Marshall, a muckraker, revealed their unsanitary conditions. In 1895, the state passed The Bakeshop Act, which aimed to prevent biscuit, cake, and bread bakers from working more than 10 hours a day or 60 hours a week.

    Twice charged with violating this statute, Lochner decided to challenge the law on the grounds that it violated the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause, which he argued protected the economic liberty to enter into such a contract with one’s employees.

    Lochner ultimately made its way to the Supreme Court and presented the court with the question of whether New York’s law violated Lochner’s fundamental liberty interest. Everyone agreed that, under the powers reserved to the states, New York certainly had some powers to regulate general welfare. The question was whether New York had gone too far in restricting an employer’s freedom to contract with his employees.

    In a recent development, for some, the New York statute was perfectly legitimate and a function of the democratic process. As then-future Judge Learned Hand argued, “we should not have the inconsistent spectacle of a government, in theory representative, which distrusted the courage and justice of its representatives, and put its faith in a [judiciary] which was, and ought to be, the least representative of popular feeling." Put simply, if there was a legitimate legislative purpose for the law, then according to Hand, courts should defer to what the elected representatives decided.

    Industry observers note that in what was seen even at the time as a surprising decision, the Supreme Court sided with Lochner five to four. “The general right to make a contract in relation to his business is part of the liberty of the individual protected by the Fourteenth Amendment of the Federal Constitution,” wrote Justice Rufus Peckham in his majority opinion.

    According to recent reports, while Peckham conceded there could be grounds for the legislature to implement regulations to improve workplace safety, he also held there was not sufficient evidence that the Bakeshop Act’s hour-limits would actually improve worker health. And if the statute was upheld, Peckham argued that it would open up almost every aspect of life to state regulation.

    In dissent, Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes lampooned the majority, writing that “a constitution is not intended to embody a particular economic theory.”.

    Lochner has since been abandoned and its reasoning rejected by most legal scholars. Yet defenders remain. Law Professor Randy Barnett, for example, argues for a theory that if the government wants to institute a regulation of liberty, “the burden of proof is more or less on the legislature.” This gets at a fundamental debate in constitutional law: Why do certain civil liberties not explicitly mentioned in the Constitution get heightened scrutiny while economic liberty does not?

    As for Lochner himself, he returned to private life and continued to run his bakery. He died on December 14, 1939.

    Recent findings suggest that roscoe Filburn: Wickard v. Filburn.

    Few cases are more detested by constitutional conservatives than Wickard v. Filburn. Roscoe Curtiss Filburn was born on August 2, 1902, in Dayton, Ohio. A fifth-generation farmer, Filburn grew crops and raised livestock. The crops included winter wheat, which was, in part, for personal use.

    In a New Deal effort to help prop up the struggling agriculture industry, Congress enacted the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938. The secretary of Agriculture would create a national allotment of acres that could be used to produce wheat. The allotment would then be appropriated to states and ultimately to individual farmers. Filburn’s allotment in 1940 was for 11.1 acres of wheat, but he planted 23 acres of it. Administrators of the AAA fined Filburn 49 cents per excess bushel that he grew and placed a lien of $117.11 on his entire wheat yield.

    Filburn challenged the excess penalty in court on the grounds that the statute was passed under the Commerce Clause, which states that Congress shall have the power to “regulate Commerce ... among the several States.” Filburn contended that his activities did not implicate interstate commerce.

    If the winter wheat was grown by Filburn and never crossed state lines, could Congress then regulate it?

    According to recent reports, the Supreme Court sided against Filburn, holding unanimously that his economic activities, taken in the aggregate, would have a substantial effect on interstate commerce. The logic went as follows: If Filburn grew his own wheat, then he would not need to purchase wheat on the open market; and if many farmers did this, it would undermine Congress’ efforts to stabilize the price of crops. “That [Filburn’s] own contribution to the demand for wheat may be trivial by itself is not enough to remove him from the scope of federal regulation where, as here, his contribution, taken together with that of many others similarly situated, is far from trivial,” explained Justice Robert Jackson.

    Industry observers note that the decision remains controversial to this day (to put it mildly). Critics of Filburn argue that the decision gives Congress near unlimited power to enact regulations under the Commerce Clause, effectively allowing Congress to regulate every aspect of people’s lives and largely mooting the powers reserved to the states. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the Supreme Court appeared ready to reduce the Commerce Clause’s reach, striking down two statutes as exceeding Congress’ power. But it has not invalidated a law on these grounds since. (Although the Supreme Court in National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius held that Congress lacked the power to enact the Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate under the Commerce Clause, it ultimately upheld the mandate under Congress’ power to tax.).

    It has been revealed that filburn returned to private life after his Supreme Court case and rarely spoke about it. During the 1950s, he purchased Beverly Shop, a woman’s beauty store, and, in 1966, Filburn convinced the other successors to his grandparent’s 640-acre farm to collectively sell the land to developers. He died on October 4, 1987, at the age of 85.

    According to recent reports, estelle Griswold: Griswold v. Connecticut.

    Estelle Griswold was born on June 8, 1900, in Hartford, Connecticut. A talented singer, she attended The Hartt School of Music, a music conservatory in Hartford. In 1935, she moved to Washington, D.C. for her husband’s job, where she volunteered at a doctor’s office and worked at George Washington University as a lab instructor.

    Industry observers note that in the 1950s, Griswold moved to Latest Haven and a few years later was offered the role of executive director of the Planned Parenthood League of Connecticut. In 1961, she opened a birth control clinic in New Haven, along with a doctor, but was convicted and fined $100 in violation of the Barnum Act, a Connecticut law that prohibited the use of “any drug, medicine, article, or instrument” to prevent conception (and, yes, named after that Barnum).

    Industry observers note that griswold challenged her conviction on the grounds that the Barnum Act was unconstitutional. As some of the act’s legal defenders pointed out, although many may regard such a law as a profound violation of personal autonomy, the Constitution lacks any mention of “privacy,” never mind preventative contraception. Put succinctly by Justice Potter Stewart in his dissenting opinion, “I can find no such general right of privacy in the Bill of Rights, in any other part of the Constitution, or in any case ever before decided by this Court.” (To be fair, the idea of the Constitution containing a right to privacy was not new when Griswold was decided; albeit in a different context, Justice Louis Brandeis had articulated such a right in an 1890 law review article.).

    In a 7-2 decision, the Supreme Court found the Barnum Act unconstitutional and held that married couples have a right to contraception as part of an implicit right to privacy. Justice William Douglas contended that the lack of its enumeration does not preclude that right from existing under the Constitution, akin to precedent in which the court found a parental right to send their children to religious schools. According to Douglas, “specific guarantees in the Bill of Rights have penumbras, formed by emanations from those guarantees that help give them life and substance. ... Various guarantees create zones of privacy.”.

    While Douglas’ vote for a constitutional right to privacy won the day, his articulation of penumbras and emanations did not fare so well (although Justice Clarence Thomas apparently still pays “tribute” to this language with a sign in his office reading “Please do not emanate into the penumbra”). Rather, concurring in the judgement, Justice John Harlan II argued that the “teachings of history [and] solid recognition of the basic values that underlie our society” based in the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause supported the decision in Griswold, a standard that has since become the prevailing defense of the right to privacy and served as a foundation for later Supreme Court decisions such as Roe v. Wade and Obergefell v. Hodges.

    Soon after the decision was unveiled, the PPLC clinic reopened, but Griswold stepped down as executive director as she had fallen out of favor with some members of the organization due to its continued financial struggles. Griswold passed away on August 13, 1981, in Fort Myers, Florida at age 81 and was posthumously inducted into the Connecticut Women’s Hall of Fame in 1994.

    Recent findings suggest that the Tinkers: Tinker v. Des Moines.

    In a recent development, another major area of constitutional controversy has involved the limits of free speech in the classroom context. Although such cases continue to crop up (BONG HiTS 4 JESUS, anyone?), the modern foundation for them was laid in 1969’s Tinker v. Des Moines. Which brings us to the Tinkers.

    John Tinker was born in 1950, and his sister, Mary Beth, was born in 1952. They grew up in Atlantic, Iowa, where their father was the pastor of a Methodist church. In November 1965, John, then a high schooler, attended a rally in opposition to the Vietnam War in Washington, D.C. On the way back to Iowa, John and other protesters agreed to wear black armbands to protest the war and to mourn the deaths on both sides.

    It has been revealed that more than 50 students across public schools in Des Moines planned to wear black armbands to school on December 16, 1965, in support of Sen. Robert Kennedy’s proposed Christmas truce. However, local principals instituted a policy that all students wearing black armbands would be asked to remove them.

    On December 16, 1965, Mary Beth wore a black armband to Warren Harding Junior High School and was suspended after she refused to take it off. The next day, John wore a black armband to North High School and was also suspended after declining to remove it.

    In March 1966, the Tinkers sued, arguing the schools violated their constitutional rights. Specifically, the Tinkers contended that the public schools were an arm of the state and they were therefore bound by the First Amendment.

    Allan Herrick, arguing for Des Moines at the Supreme Court, contended that the school district must be in a position to “preserve order and to avoid this disturbance and disruption in the school room.” As Justice Thomas would argue decades later in Morse v. Frederick, “through the legal doctrine of in loco parentis [in the place of a parent], courts [historically] upheld the right of schools to discipline students, to enforce rules, and to maintain order.”.

    In February 1969, the Supreme Court sided with the Tinkers, holding that students do not “shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate.” In its decision, written by Justice Abe Fortas, the court established the substantial disruption test, which sets the necessary conditions for regulating student speech. To do so, the school must be able to reasonably foretell “material and substantial interference” with other students’ learning or the school’s operations. Fortas held that the school district failed to show that the Tinkers’ protests resulted in any material disruption.

    To this day, Tinker receives mixed reviews. Supporters of an expansive interpretation of the First Amendment tend to support the principles in Tinker and argue that they should be even more broadly applied; critics, such as Justice Thomas, are skeptical that students have First Amendment rights at all. (As Justice Hugo Black put it in his Tinker dissent, “It may be that the Nation has outworn the old-fashioned slogan that ‘children are to be seen, not heard,’ but one may, I hope, be permitted to harbor the thought that taxpayers send children to school on the premise that, at their age, they need to learn, not teach.”).

    After the Supreme Court’s decision, John Tinker remained active in anti-Vietnam war demonstrations and later became the manager of KPIP-LP 94.7 FM, a local radio station, which he manages to this day. Mary Beth Tinker pursued a career in medicine, working as a pediatric and emergency room nurse and a nurse practitioner. In 2013, Mary Beth left the nursing field and embarked on the “Tinker Tour,” where she travels the country telling her story and promoting civic education to young people.

    Clarence Brandenburg: Brandenburg v. Ohio.

    According to recent reports, let’s conclude with our least likable plaintiff, who nevertheless established one of the most enduring Supreme Court precedents. Clarence Brandenburg was born on March 3, 1916, in Lee County, Kentucky. A Marine Corps veteran, he worked at a General Electric plant and operated a television repair shop upon returning to civilian life. After declaring personal bankruptcy in 1959, Brandenburg began getting involved with white supremacist organizations and sought to become a leader of the KKK.

    In June 1964, Brandenburg spoke at a Klan rally, which was shown on a local television station. Brandenburg said “We're not a revengent organization, but if our President, our Congress, our Supreme Court, continues to suppress the white, Caucasian race, it's possible that there might have to be some revengeance taken. ... We are marching on Congress July the Fourth, four hundred thousand strong.” He was then charged with violating Ohio’s criminal syndicalism statute prohibiting advocating “sabotage, violence, or ... terrorism ... as a means of accomplishing ... political reform,” and later convicted.

    Brandenburg appealed, arguing that his speech was protected by the First Amendment. Specifically, he argued that Ohio could not punish him for advocating for unlawful action without showing that his speech was directed towards producing such action.

    Leonard Kirschner, arguing on behalf of Ohio at the Supreme Court, asserted that Brandenburg’s actions were not conducted in isolation and could lead to violence, contending that “the statements [made by Brandenburg] to 10 or 20 people can cause one heck of a lot of crime and violence and terrorism in any community. It only takes one person to cause it.”.

    In a recent development, the Supreme Court reversed Brandenburg’s conviction in 1969 on First Amendment grounds. According to the court, the Ohio statute in question failed to distinguish between an abstract endorsement of unlawful activity and speech directed towards producing imminent, lawless action. In doing so, the court established what became known as the Brandenburg test, which required that speech sufficient for incitement be “directed to inciting or producing imminent lawless action” and “likely to incite or produce such action.”.

    In a recent development, in 1971, Brandenburg was found guilty of harassing his Jewish neighbor by repeatedly calling him and uttering antisemitic slurs. He died on March 29, 1986.

    They came from different backgrounds, had very different worldviews, and dealt with different issues, but each of these plaintiffs had one thing in common: pushing up against the limits of state power. How that power manifested itself differed considerably, as did the court’s willingness to reign it in. For example, while the court has advanced a highly protective understanding of the First Amendment, it has been more hesitant to advance protections of economic liberty.

    The nature of the plaintiff also mattered less in these cases than one might presume. Filburn was a farmer who grew wheat for his own personal consumption but did not prevail at the court. Brandenburg, on the other hand, expressed white supremacist ideas yet proved successful before the justices, becoming responsible for an entirely upcoming free speech doctrine.

    Some may view the court blinding itself to the actual facts on the ground as too simplistic; others as an ideal to aspire to. On that note, we’ll give Justice Elena Kagan the final word: “the question is not do you like this party or do you like that party ... the question is what the law requires.”.

    Blake Fox is an intern for SCOTUSblog.

    #204536. Which justices favor the Trump administration the most (and least) on the emergency docket?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2016 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Which justices favor the Trump administration the most (and least) on the emergency docket?

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook in June, the justices divided in a manner that would have been difficult to predict from some perceptions of the court.
    • Four months later, the administration lost another emergency application, this time in a dispute over medical care for transgender federal prisoners.
    • According to recent reports, the contrast points to a recurring theme of the Supreme Court’s emergency decisions: Although the conservative justices are often lumped together as “pro-Trump,” their rulings can depend on whether the dispute concerns immigration, presidential removal authority, federal spending, or the scope of emergency relief.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s attempt to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook in June, the justices divided in a manner that would have been difficult to predict from some perceptions of the court. Chief Justice John Roberts and Justice Brett Kavanaugh joined Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson to leave Cook in office while the case proceeded. Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, and Amy Coney Barrett dissented. The administration lost, but the court’s disagreement did not reflect the familiar ideological split.

    Four months later, the administration lost another emergency application, this time in a dispute over medical care for transgender federal prisoners. In Trump v. Kingdom, Thomas and Alito indicated that they would have granted the requested stay, but no other justice publicly held that position. Unlike Trump v. Cook, which produced a signed opinion after oral argument, the Kingdom order disclosed nothing about the reasoning or votes behind the court’s denial.

    According to recent reports, the contrast points to a recurring theme of the Supreme Court’s emergency decisions: Although the conservative justices are often lumped together as “pro-Trump,” their rulings can depend on whether the dispute concerns immigration, presidential removal authority, federal spending, or the scope of emergency relief. And whereas some justices have supported federal executive positions at broadly similar rates across presidencies, others appear far more likely to do so depending on whether the president is a Republican or Democrat.

    It has been revealed that the prior article in this series examined how frequently the Trump and Biden administrations prevailed. In turning to the individual justices, I reviewed federal executive-action decisions from 2017 through November 12, 2026, consolidated into 106 distinct substantive decisions. The three administrations account for 32, 36, and 38 decisions, respectively.

    Recent findings suggest that there is a very notable qualification throughout: the court often publishes emergency orders without identifying each justice’s vote. The analysis thus assigned a justice to the court’s majority ruling when they were silent, absent an express position or other evidence indicating otherwise.

    So what can we say about the different justices’ support for the Trump administration on the emergency docket?

    Different presidents, different justices.

    In a recent development, the most consistent record belongs to Roberts. He aligned with federal executive positions in 23 of 31 eligible decisions during Trump’s first administration, 26 of 36 under Biden, and 28 of 38 during Trump’s second administration. Those figures amount to 74%, 72%, and 74%. The disputes changed markedly, but Roberts’ aggregate willingness to leave the federal government’s position intact – or grant it relief – barely moved. In other words, Roberts has typically supported executive power on the emergency docket regardless of who is president.

    The next most consistent justice, Barrett (though with a much lower sample size), aligned with Biden in 69% of her eligible decisions and Trump II in 78%. Third was Kavanaugh, with rates of 78%, 67%, and 79%. Then came Gorsuch, with rates of 83%, 54%, and 84%.

    It has been revealed that thomas and Alito present a very different picture. Thomas supported the executive in 83% of eligible Trump I decisions, 39% under Biden, and 92% under Trump II. Alito’s corresponding figures were 83%, 47%, and 92%.

    It has been revealed that the liberal justices show the opposite movement, although their individual records differ. Kagan supported executive positions in 43% of eligible Trump I decisions, 94% under Biden, and 24% under Trump II. Sotomayor’s rates were 27%, 94%, and 16%. Jackson, who joined the court during Biden’s presidency, supported its executive position in 21 of 24 eligible decisions (88%), compared with three of 38 (8%) under Trump II.

    Recent findings suggest that the figure above makes these distinctions particularly clear. Roberts remains between 72% and 74% across the three periods, while Thomas’ support moves from 83% under Trump I to 39% under Biden and 92% under Trump II. The middle group of Barrett, Kavanaugh, and Gorsuch is more varied, but each supported Biden’s executive position more frequently than a simple Republican-versus-Democratic framing might suggest.

    In a recent development, these numbers are telling, but they do not establish the reasons for why the justices decided as they did. For example, a president defending an environmental rule presents a very different legal issue from one seeking permission to remove an independent agency official. To determine how much of the observed variation is associated with presidential identity, the next step is to examine the kinds of cases that produced it.

    The complications that unite and divide the justices.

    In a recent development, immigration provides a useful point of comparison because it generated substantial emergency litigation under all three administrations. Roberts supported the executive in 10 of 11 immigration decisions under Trump I, three of six under Biden, and 11 of 13 under Trump II. Thomas supported the government in 10 of 10 eligible Trump I immigration decisions, two of six under Biden, and 12 of 13 under Trump II. Kagan’s comparable figures were six of eleven, six of six, and five of 13.

    Recent findings suggest that this is revealing. Roberts and Thomas both supported Trump’s immigration positions at high rates but not as much when Biden defended his administration’s policies. Kagan and Sotomayor supported Biden in all six coded immigration decisions, then opposed most of Trump II positions. But there is, of course, a key caveat: This category covers different immigration rules, as opposed to simple support for one president over another.

    Public-health and related health litigation under Biden revealed a sharper division within the conservative majority. In 10 eligible health-coded decisions, Roberts and Kavanaugh each supported the federal executive in seven, compared with one each for Thomas and Alito. Barrett supported it in five; Gorsuch in two. Kagan and Sotomayor each supported the government in nine such cases. (Jackson’s two favorable positions came from only three eligible decisions in this category, making her figure much less informative.).

    The court’s January 2022 vaccination decisions supply a concrete example. Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the liberals in allowing the administration to enforce a vaccination requirement for workers at healthcare facilities receiving Medicare or Medicaid funding, while Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett dissented. On the same day, Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the conservatives in blocking OSHA’s broader vaccination-or-testing standard. To Roberts and Kavanaugh, health litigation was clearly treated issue-by-issue.

    Industry observers note that let’s move on to personnel decisions, or the president’s control over the executive branch. In the nine Trump II personnel and removal decisions, Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett supported the executive in eight, while Roberts and Kavanaugh did so in seven. In four foreign-affairs and national-security decisions, Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch aligned with the government in all of these, compared with two for Roberts and Barrett.

    Subject matter therefore helps explain how things break down. The same conservative justice may support emergency intervention in a dispute over immigration enforcement while resisting it in a case involving agency regulation. The legal authority being asserted, the posture of the case, and the requested remedy all shape the decision.

    The coalitions inside the conservative majority.

    It has been revealed that so which justices most frequently aligned? At the front of the pack are Thomas and Alito, who agreed in all 38 coded Trump II decisions. Their alignment is particularly visible when the administration lost. In seven events, both of their positions favored more relief for the administration than the majority granted or would otherwise provide.

    Other pairings are almost as cohesive. Roberts and Barrett agreed in 35 of 36 Trump II decisions (97%). Roberts and Kavanaugh agreed in 36 of 38 of these (95%), as did Gorsuch and Kavanaugh. The next figure displays those pairings alongside the liberal and cross-ideological relationships. The high agreement rates show how often the conservatives arrive at the same apparent disposition, but the exceptions reveal competing views about the scope of emergency judicial intervention.

    Recent findings suggest that the foreign-assistance dispute in Department of State v. AIDS Vaccine Advocacy Coalition, for instance, separated Roberts and Barrett from Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Kavanaugh. The four dissenters would have granted the administration relief from an order requiring payment for foreign-aid work already completed. Roberts and Barrett did not join that position. Their disagreement concerned what a district court could require of the government while the underlying funding litigation continued.

    In a recent development, A different alignment emerged in NIH v. American Public Health Association. There, the court granted partial relief in litigation over terminated research grants. Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Kavanaugh would have granted the administration’s request in full, while Roberts joined Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson in seeking to deny it altogether. Barrett supported an intermediate outcome.

    According to recent reports, in Cook, the division shifted again. Roberts and Kavanaugh joined the liberals in rejecting the administration’s attempt to immediately remove a Federal Reserve governor, while Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, and Barrett dissented. In Trump v. Illinois, concerning the Trump administration’s deployment of National Guard forces, Thomas, Alito, and Gorsuch disagreed with the court’s denial of relief to Trump, while Kavanaugh concurred in the judgment on narrower grounds.

    The evidence points toward distinctive approaches to removal authority, spending, the judicial supervision of agencies, and emergency remedies. Justices who agree in one field can diverge in another, and partial orders sometimes put a justice between two groups seeking opposing forms of relief.

    The liberal justices and the unusual alliances across ideological lines.

    The three liberal justices also exhibited some meaningful disagreements. Under Trump II, Jackson aligned with the executive in only three of 38 emergency decisions (8%), compared with six for Sotomayor (16%) and nine for Kagan (24%). Kagan and Sotomayor agreed in 35 of 38 such decisions; Kagan and Jackson in 32. The differences are not as dramatic as those dividing the conservatives, but they complicate the assumption that the liberal trio behaves as a single bloc in every emergency dispute.

    Their publicly registered dissents differ as well. Jackson expressly opposed a Trump II executive position in 26 decisions, Sotomayor in 23, and Kagan in 20. In FCC v. Brown, for example, Sotomayor and Jackson publicly indicated that they would deny the agency’s stay application, while Kagan registered no public disagreement.

    According to recent reports, trump’s second term has produced more than one identifiable cross-ideological alignment. The five-justice majority in Cook included Roberts, Kavanaugh, and the three liberals, while the NIH grants dispute placed Roberts and the liberals together against complete relief. Barrett also joined certain portions of Sotomayor’s dissent in Trump v. J.G.G., a dispute involving the Alien Enemies Act, although her partial join should not necessarily be counted as agreement with the liberals on the case.

    These examples again highlight why the distinction between shared results and shared legal reasoning is key. A justice can favor the same outcome as an ideological opponent while arriving there for entirely different reasons (we see this with concurrences in merits cases all the time). Separate opinions can also reveal agreement on a particular procedural or statutory question even when the justices disagree on the ultimate relief. At the same time, the emergency docket makes these relationships especially difficult to measure comprehensively because many orders contain no individual vote information at all.

    My analysis of the emergency docket reveals a chief most reluctant to favor one administration over another, with Barrett and Kavanaugh following closely behind; Gorsuch acting more favorably towards the Trump administration, although not overwhelmingly so; Thomas and Alito disproportionately favoring Trump over Biden; and the three liberal justices acting as a near mirror image of Thomas and Alito – although to varied degrees.

    We thus see a conservative majority whose members separate over particular exercises of federal power, a liberal bloc with distinguishable voting and dissent records, and occasional alliances that cross ideological lines.

    Dr. Adam Feldman is the creator and author of the blog Empirical SCOTUS and the Substack Legalytics.

    #204535. Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2109 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Refugees, asylum, and Supreme Court exceptionalism

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American exceptionalism, the idea that the United States is uniquely virtuous, has deep roots that predate the nation itself.
    • According to recent reports, at best, American exceptionalism can be beneficent in intent and beneficial in result.
    • According to recent reports, and then there is the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American exceptionalism, the idea that the United States is uniquely virtuous, has deep roots that predate the nation itself. The founders of Latest England, in words echoed by President Ronald Reagan, famously declared that it was to be “as a citty upon a Hill. The eies of all people are upon us.”.

    According to recent reports, at best, American exceptionalism can be beneficent in intent and beneficial in result. In time the New England states would become leaders in the abolition of slavery. Closer to our time, the United States would translate its victory in the Second Word War into the Marshall Initiative, the World Bank, and the presently embattled international legal order under the aegis of the United Nations. The 18th Amendment, the juvenile death penalty (until 2005), and the failure to guarantee a right to healthcare furnish examples of exceptionalism gone wrong.

    According to recent reports, and then there is the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law. At the Founding and for decades thereafter, the court tended to embrace “the law of nations,” either as a guide to interpreting relevant statutes or even as furnishing a rule of decision in appropriate circumstances. In more recent times, however, majorities have balked at viewing treaties as self-executing, taking guidance from the International Court of Justice, or applying statutes that expressly incorporate “the law of nations” into domestic law.

    A grant of certiorari just this month will likely confirm the trend. The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, in which the justices will review one of the Trump administration’s earliest attempts to restrict immigration. On the administration’s first day, a presidential proclamation declared that “an invasion is ongoing on the southern border.” The proclamation, among other things, sought to suspend entry to the United States for non-citizens “engaged in the invasion,” even for refugees fleeing persecution and seeking to apply for asylum. But the edict went one step further. It also mandated expedited removal to asylum seekers who had crossed the border seeking to apply for asylum and provided for expedited removal of such persons.

    Sources indicate that the proclamation was issued notwithstanding a congressional framework that seeks to facilitate asylum – indefinite lawful residence – to those escaping persecution in their home country, set forth primarily in the 1952 Immigration and Nationality Act as amended by the 1980 Refugee Act and later amendments (codified under Title 8 of the U.S. Code). This framework: a) ensures a right to apply for asylum, b) links eligibility for asylum to refugee status, and c) provides protections against the government removing persons who would be likely to face persecution or torture.

    Section 1158 establishes the right to seek asylum. It provides that “[a]ny alien who is physically present in the United States … irrespective of such alien’s status, may apply for asylum.” The same section makes eligibility for asylum conditional, among other things, on a demonstration of refugee status. For this the statute relies on the definition of refugee in section 1101(a)(42) as a person who is unwilling or unable to return to their home country “because of persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.”.

    Industry observers note that in turn, safeguards from removal come from two sources. The immigration statute itself states that noncitizens cannot be removed to a country where the attorney general determines that the “alien’s life or freedom would be threatened in that country because of the alien’s race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion.” In addition, the Foreign Affairs Reform & Restructuring Act of 1998 restricts removal to a country when “there are substantial grounds for believing the person would be in danger of being subjected to torture.”.

    The Trump administration initially justified the denial of asylum and removal protections to those within the United States by invoking the president’s authority to suspend entry “of any aliens or of any class of aliens into the United States [that] would be detrimental to the interests of the United States.” The logic is that no one who violated the suspension by entering should be entitled to asylum and removal protections. To this defense the administration has added the formal role of the attorney general and director of Homeland Security. The INA grants each official the authority to grant asylum to eligible applicants as well as withhold removal for those who qualify. At the same time, the statute makes clear that these decisions are subject to individualized judicial review under an “abuse of discretion” standard. (At least until the second Trump administration, decisions not to grant relief to those who had demonstrated that they had qualified for asylum were the “exceedingly rare“ exception.).

    In a recent development, the lower courts rejected both justifications. Judge Randolph Moss of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia dismissed the administration’s claim that the president’s suspension of entry to those “engaged in [the] invasion” invalidated asylum and removal protections that expressly applied to persons physically in the country. The D.C. Circuit agreed with a slightly different emphasis. Writing for the majority, Judge Michelle Childs also rejected the idea that a suspension of entry justified eliminating asylum and removal safeguards for those present in the United States. To this point she added that, as a grant of asylum is discretionary, the express right to apply it entails individualized consideration rather than blanket elimination. (Judge Justin Walker issued a partial dissenting argument that the grant of discretionary authority permits a blanket denial of asylum claims.).

    The D.C. courts’ holdings are not wrong so far as they go. Suspending entry would appear to be a different power from removing someone after they had entered. The provisions for asylum strongly imply individualized consideration and even suggest a presumption of granting asylum to those who meet the detailed eligibility requirements. The relevant provisions plainly bar removal of those who qualify for that protection. But whether this reasoning will be sufficient at the Supreme Court is another matter. This is so not least given the justices’ recent penchant for giving the executive wide latitude on immigration.

    But the justices should take into account some additional perspective.

    One relevant perspective comes from international law. Surprising as it may seem, the United States is not exceptional in having to grapple with immigration, refugees, and asylum. More surprising still, these common global challenges has yielded what should be familiar, common legal standards that apply, and to a great extent which owe their development to, the United States. Perhaps most surprising of all, standard domestic doctrines invite reference to this body of law when interpreting applicable federal statutes.

    Consider first asylum. As an initial matter, the domestic asylum framework incorporates international standards as a function of congressional intent. As the court itself recognized in 1987’s INS v. Cardozo-Fonseca, Congress enacted the Refugee Act of 1980 to bring U.S. law in conformity with the nation’s obligations as a state party to the 1967 Protocol to the 1951 Refugee Convention. Crucially, in determining those obligations, the court sensibly drew upon the views of the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Refugees.

    What do those obligations contemplate? The Refugee Conventions do not expressly provide for a right to apply for long-term asylum, as opposed to specifying rights for refugees fleeing persecution. But the UNCHR has maintained that international law presupposes individualized consideration of refugee status, especially before that status is denied. Given that Congress made the requirements for refugee status the basis for being eligible for asylum, it would be odd to conclude that the U.S. would remain in conformity with the convention as interpreted by the UN’s most authoritative body should the executive reject the right to seek asylum by means of a categorial denial of all asylum claims.

    Not surprisingly, categorical rejection of asylum claims would also be at variance with widespread international practice, especially as mandated in Europe. And neither last nor least, the administration’s position would also be inconsistent with the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights’ express guarantee of a right to asylum. Though not binding, the UDHR was adopted without dissent by the UN General Assembly, reflects the dominant position of the Member States, and informs their practice.

    Recent findings suggest that the Charming Betsy canon leads to the same conclusion. In the 1804 case Murray v. the Schooner Charming Betsy, Chief Justice John Marshall famously stated that “an act of Congress ought never to be construed to violate the law of nations if any other possible construction remains.” Marshall’s reference to the “law of nations” is generally understood to apply to modern customary international law. International custom arises given a near consensus of state practice perused out of a sense of legal obligation.

    In a recent development, section 1158’s grant of authority to the executive to grant asylum applications can be construed at least in two ways. It might mean a complete categorical discretion to deny. Or it might be better understood to assume individualized consideration. The latter clearly better comports with international practice. Yet there is even a stronger consideration. Customary, and for that matter treaty law, clearly prohibits removal to countries where a refugee has a well-founded fear of facing persecution or torture. When the result is expedited removal, the categorical denial of asylum status to persons claiming to escape from persecution and torture places the U.S. in obvious jeopardy of violating exactly this well-established international prohibition.

    Sources indicate that which brings up the matter of removal itself. Here the upshot of Congress’ intent is more direct. Article 33.1 of the 1951 Refugee Convention provides: “No Contracting State shall expel or return (“refouler”) a refugee in any manner whatsoever to the frontiers of territories where his life or freedom would be threatened on account of his race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion.” Likewise, Article 3.1 of the Convention Against Torture mandates that “No State Party shall expel, return ("refouler") or extradite a person to another State where there are substantial grounds for believing that he would be in danger of being subjected to torture.” As noted, the Refugee Act in the first instance sought to place the U.S. in conformity with the Refugee Convention. FARRA sought to do the same with CAT. Categorically removing persons in the U.S. seeking asylum all but guarantees violations of the treaties that Congress sought to uphold.

    According to recent reports, so strong is the congressional intent argument that the Charming Betsy need not set sail. Yet even if the relevant statutory provisions were somehow ambiguous, the Charming Betsy canon would compel rejection of the administration’s position. Assume that section 1182(f), which grants the executive discretion to deny asylum claims, authorizes a categorial denial of applications across the board. Assume further that this section, along with section 1185(a)(1), can be read to permit removal of persons within the United States denied the opportunity to apply for asylum on the basis of persecution or torture. Even without the conventions, international practice has separately established “non-refoulement” – the prohibition of returning, or “refouling,” a person to return to a territory where he may be exposed to persecution as a matter of binding customary international law. Reading the relevant statutes to permit removal would then constitute a clear violation of non-refoulement. That reading would therefore also run counter to the Charming Betsy canon.

    Industry observers note that A sad yet likely irony is that Mullin v. RAICES will privilege one strand of American exceptionalism over another. Much of the international law relevant to the case reflects the nation’s exceptional effort to leverage its dominance after the Second World War not to establish a traditional empire, but to construct a rules-based international order. One of many achievements was the 1951 Refugee Convention, like the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, brought about in no small part thanks to the efforts of Eleanor Roosevelt as a U.S. representative to the UN. Against this is the view that America has little to heed from the rest of the world, including on matters that implicate international affairs. The court adopted this stance on immigration as recently as last term. We shall see which view prevails.

    Martin Flaherty is Charles and Marie Robertson Visiting Professor at the School of Public and International Affairs at Princeton, and Leitner Family Professor Chair of International Human Rights Law at Fordham Law School in Upcoming York.

    #204533. Breaking: Supreme Court defers decision on whether to dismiss major gun case

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (480 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Supreme Court defers decision on whether to dismiss major gun case

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (480 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With just over a week remaining before the justices will hear oral argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy.
    • Recent findings suggest that the skirmish over whether the Illinois case should still go forward began on October 29, when Cutberto Viramontes, the named plaintiff in the case, filed a motion seeking to be dismissed from the case.
    • Recent findings suggest that lawyers for Cook County subsequently asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the case as moot, arguing that it is “doubtful” that any of the other challengers would have a legal right to sue.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With just over a week remaining before the justices will hear oral argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy. The court’s brief, unsigned order, which came one day after the justices granted a request by the lead plaintiff to remove him from the case, indicated that the justices would instead “defer[]” that ruling “pending oral argument,” which is scheduled for Wednesday, December 2.

    Recent findings suggest that the skirmish over whether the Illinois case should still go forward began on October 29, when Cutberto Viramontes, the named plaintiff in the case, filed a motion seeking to be dismissed from the case. Viramontes, who has been part of the challenge since it was filed in 2021, did not provide any explanation for his request.

    Recent findings suggest that lawyers for Cook County subsequently asked the Supreme Court to dismiss the case as moot, arguing that it is “doubtful” that any of the other challengers would have a legal right to sue. They emphasized that Viramontes was a Cook County resident who said that he wanted to own an AR-15-style semiautomatic rifle. By contrast, they wrote, the other individual challenger in the case, Christopher Khaya, has said that he wants to own “an IMI Galil semiautomatic rifle,” which, according to Cook County, is not the kind of AR-15-style rifle covered by the question before the court.

    The challengers countered that the question presented is not limited to AR-15 rifles but also extends to “similar” semiautomatic rifles, which would include AK-47-style rifles like the IMI Galil. But in any event, they added, Khaya “also desires to possess an AR-15 platform rifle and would acquire one if it were lawful for him to do so.”.

    It has been revealed that in its order deferring a decision on whether the Cook County case is moot because of the dismissal of Viramontes from the case, the Supreme Court cited its 2023 decision in Acheson Hotels, LLC v. Laufer, in which it unanimously agreed after oral argument that the case was moot because the plaintiff had voluntarily dismissed her lawsuit in the lower court. But the chances that the court will ultimately reach the merits of the ban are likely higher than in Acheson, in which there was only one plaintiff, because the dispute over semiautomatic rifles encompasses not only multiple plaintiffs but also another case – a challenge to Connecticut’s ban on AR-15-style rifles.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    Latest Update: Why Mobile Apps Treasure Downtime; Terms Of Non-Endearment

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (693 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.
    • According to recent reports, but wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for users’ downtime?
    • People using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mobile games compete with social media and streaming for attention in the cutthroat worlds of viral feeds and app marketplaces.

    According to recent reports, but wouldn’t it make more sense for these apps to compete for users’ downtime? That’s the case made by Felix Braberg, a mobile ad and monetization consultant, in a blog post.

    People using apps like DoorDash and Uber, for instance, “have nothing to do while they wait,” as Braberg puts it. Meanwhile, both DoorDash and Uber have billion-dollar annual ad businesses, but they’re not rushing to build their own gaming or streaming offerings. So they’re natural fits for app advertisers looking to help consumers pass the time.

    Sources indicate that appLovin’s strength in mobile gaming is not so dissimilar. But AppLovin has a nascent consumer advertising segment now, and a few of its early advertisers have noted the power of reaching people while they’re playing games on the toilet. It doesn’t get more “downtime” than that.

    Gaming can fit neatly into the downtime vacuum that right now is awkwardly filled by ads or nothing. But successfully advertising a mobile game traditionally required a user to download the game and leave the app where they saw it advertised.

    Now, though, startups such as PlaysOut are integrating mobile games directly into other apps and monetizing those experiences with rewarded video. It’s a way for nongaming apps to capitalize on the downtime that benefits gaming.

    Which leads Braberg to predict that the next wave of mobile growth “will come from apps that were never game companies.”.

    Scarcely a week after launching ChatGPT’s new Business Hub, designed to let businesses see how they’re performing in ChatGPT, OpenAI has revised the Hub’s terms of service, Digiday reports.

    The revisions came soon after Digiday reached out to OpenAI, citing legal concerns brought forward by lawyers on behalf of publishers.

    Sources indicate that some of those legal restrictions have been removed in the revised terms of service. However, the revised terms also introduced more restrictions, such as requiring companies to waive their right to seek a court order preventing OpenAI from using certain customer data.

    But, while OpenAI is still imposing some legal restrictions on companies that use its Business Hub, “they don’t leave a customer completely without recourse,” an IP and tech lawyer who requested anonymity tells Digiday. “A customer could still, even if not entirely practical, sue for monetary damages.”.

    According to recent reports, the Italian conglomerate Bending Spoons has been amassing a collection of consumer- and business-facing software vendors that kind of resembles the Island of Misfit Toys. It added another dud (or stud?) to its stable last week.

    Bending Spoons will acquire Mailchimp from Intuit for about $3.7 billion, less than a third of what Intuit paid a decade ago, Reuters reports.

    Sources indicate that bending Spoons also recently added the online whiteboard Miro and location-based pet-tracking service Tractive, plus once-promising internet companies Brightcove, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo and AOL. Its business model is akin to private equity, in that it acquires struggling companies and drastically reduces headcount while raising prices or removing free tiers. Interestingly, advertising is an ancillary part of its model.

    To be clear, AOL and Vimeo haven’t quit on ad revenue. But Bending Spoons is focused on subscription revenue growth and consolidated cost savings, rather than building an identity spine for advertising and data sales.

    Industry observers note that but Bending Spoons still must demonstrate that it can turn flatlined businesses (Mailchimp declined year over year, for instance) into earners. Which is a bit like trying to bend a spoon using only your mind.

    Great news on the turnaround front: Bending Spoons reported 125% revenue growth last week.

    Sources indicate that but there’s some not-so-great news, too: Its organic growth was an anemic 3%. So growth is coming from net-upcoming businesses, with these acquisitions contributing some $4 billion in debt.

    Apple is developing its own autonomous AI agents. [Bloomberg].

    Will Anthropic eventually launch an ads business? [Digiday].

    Recent findings suggest that the Nasdaq enters its third correction of 2026 amid a painful tech investor slide. [NYT].

    A year in review of agency pitches. [Ad Age].

    #204529. The Trade Desk Can Win Again By Embracing Objectivity And Letting Go Of The Open Web

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1042 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Adexchanger ↗ Open Full Page

    The Trade Desk Can Win Again By Embracing Objectivity And Letting Go Of The Open Web

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Adexchanger

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Wall Street loves to pile on ad tech.
    • No manufacturer has felt the highs and lows of being public quite like The Trade Desk (TTD), which, outside of AppLovin and the Magnificent 7, is the best company to emerge from the ad tech sector in the last 25 years.
    • Sources indicate that TTD was built on a brilliant principle: that brands and agencies should be able to decide where their media dollars go without the firm selling the media sitting in the room.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Wall Street loves to pile on ad tech. They’re all about you when you’re up and quick to dismiss you when you’re down.

    No manufacturer has felt the highs and lows of being public quite like The Trade Desk (TTD), which, outside of AppLovin and the Magnificent 7, is the best company to emerge from the ad tech sector in the last 25 years.

    Sources indicate that TTD was built on a brilliant principle: that brands and agencies should be able to decide where their media dollars go without the firm selling the media sitting in the room. That idea remains true, and it is the reason TTD became the largest independent DSP in the world.

    Industry observers note that so what changed? TTD latched onto a latest principle: the defense of the open internet. Which means the company built its core value prop around a shrinking portion of where consumers spend their time and where advertisers spend their money.

    In a recent development, as DV360 became Google’s Death Star, The Trade Desk was the Rebel Alliance standing up for the open web. But while TTD spent the last several years proving they were the anti-Google, Amazon snuck in the back door and changed the whole DSP market.

    According to recent reports, if The Trade Desk holds to its first principle and lets go of the second, its value becomes more obvious than ever. Three moves would signal a fresh era for the firm:.

    According to recent reports, 1. Separate the value prop of “open internet” with objective decisioning. The company should retire the open internet as its stated purpose and replace it with what all advertisers value: independent, data-driven decisioning for brands and agencies. The open web stays in the portfolio as one channel among several, allowing buyers to see the whole field.

    2. Offer an objective view of the walled gardens. Google will not let a third-party DSP bid on YouTube, and Meta has shown no interest in opening its auction. But neither fact prevents The Trade Desk from ingesting platform reporting, independent measurement and content data from nearly every walled garden, then normalizing it against its own CTV and open web buys.

    Sources indicate that 3. Save the open internet by showing the whole picture. TTD taking an objective view of all platforms would highlight measurement and quality discrepancies. Which would, in turn, improve the open internet’s reputation in the eyes of the buy side. Without that full view, there is no way to show how “premium” open internet performs against the largest user-generated platforms in the world.

    From the beginning, The Trade Desk owned no inventory at all. It had no financial reason to steer a dollar anywhere except where the data said it would work for the buyer.

    TTD’s 2016 S-1 organized the company’s strengths under headings like “We Do Not Arbitrage Advertising Inventory” and “We Are Data-Driven.” The phrase “open internet” does not appear in the company’s prospectus summary or risk factors at all.

    The business built on that positioning worked extremely well. TTD went public in September 2016, grew revenue from $308 million in 2017 to $2.44 billion in 2024, reached a market cap of roughly $40 billion by 2021 and met or beat expectations for 33 consecutive quarters.

    In a recent development, in 2025, growth slowed and stock performance followed suit. That slowing growth is the natural effect of being the Pied Piper of the shrinking “open web.”.

    Redseer Strategy Consultants estimate that the programmatic open web gets only 20%-30% of ad budgets, with 70%-80% of programmatic spend going to walled gardens. This split has held for roughly five years.

    Sources indicate that advertisers have already made their decision. Budgets did not follow time spent, because walled gardens offer simplicity that programmatic cannot: an easy button for efficient reach. While the value of that reach can be debated, the easy way won.

    The concentration of spend is still increasing. EMarketer expects Google, Meta and Amazon to take 62.3% of worldwide digital ad spend in 2026, with Meta at about $243 billion and Google at about $240 billion. Amazon is forecast to grow from $69 billion in 2025 to $97 billion in 2027. Every incremental dollar in those forecasts is a dollar that an independent DSP cannot bid on today. Forecasts are growing faster than the open web.

    It has been revealed that television was supposed to be the market where the “open internet” reclaimed ground with upper-funnel brands. Except CTV is also becoming a walled garden medium. In Nielsen’s May 2026 Gauge, YouTube accounted for 13.8% of all US TV viewing, making Google the single largest media distributor in the US.

    According to recent reports, advertisers have limited transparency into the AI products of each walled garden. The content itself is UGC (and increasingly AI-generated). The measurement is dictated by the platform. And yet marketers need to spend there in order to get reach and efficiency. Imagine if there were a truly objective way to spend those dollars?

    None of this means that TTD’s founding principle failed. It means the principle is aimed at an open web target that keeps getting smaller. An objective buyer that can only see 20%-30% of the budget is no longer willing to spend the time, money and energy on the shrinking pie.

    CMOs have one budget. The question they actually want answered is where the next dollar should go across YouTube, Meta, TikTok, Snap, CTV and the web, backed by objective data. Today, nobody independently answers that question. The Trade Desk is the only firm in the industry that is poised to provide a solution.

    Most turnarounds require a company to find a new reason to exist, and most of them fail because the new reason is never as convincing as the original one. This turnaround just requires The Trade Desk to remember its original reason for being.

    When The Trade Desk opens up its view beyond the open web, Wall Street – and the buy side – will rejoice.

    Tech Report: Heading into the Thanksgiving break

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Happy Thanksgiving eve, SCOTUStoday readers!
    • According to recent reports, following the Thanksgiving break, the court’s December argument session will begin, on Monday, November 30.
    • In a recent development, on Monday, the Supreme Court dismissed lead plaintiff Cutberto Viramontes from the case formerly known as Viramontes v.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Happy Thanksgiving eve, SCOTUStoday readers! We are very grateful for your support of our work. If you’d like to learn more about what the Supreme Court has said about Thanksgiving, you can revisit our Closer Look on the topic from this time last year.

    According to recent reports, following the Thanksgiving break, the court’s December argument session will begin, on Monday, November 30. The justices will hear eight total oral arguments during this session, addressing such problems as the Second Amendment, deportations to “third-party countries,” and the seizure of an airplane over the illegal transportation of beer.

    In a recent development, on Monday, the Supreme Court dismissed lead plaintiff Cutberto Viramontes from the case formerly known as Viramontes v. Cook County, on whether the Second Amendment guarantees a right to possess AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles, but it did not take action on Cook County’s request to dismiss the case as moot. On Tuesday, the court unveiled that it had deferred action on that request until after oral argument, which will take place on Wednesday, December 2. The case name is now Khaya v. Cook County. For more on Tuesday’s announcement, see the On Site section below.

    The Supreme Court Building will be closed tomorrow and Friday for Thanksgiving.

    The December argument session will begin on Monday. That day, the justices will hear oral arguments in two cases: Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia, on whether Title IX, the federal law that prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding, allows school employees to bring lawsuits alleging sex discrimination; and Wassily v. Blanche, on whether immigrants whose asylum protections have been terminated remain eligible to become lawful permanent residents, also known as green card holders.

    Sources indicate that on Tuesday, the justices will hear argument in Jouppi v. Alaska, an Alaskan bush pilot’s challenge to the forfeiture of his $95,000 airplane over the transport of beer into a dry village.

    Industry observers note that on Wednesday, December 2, the court will hear argument in Khaya v. Cook County, on the constitutionality of bans on AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles, at 10:00 a.m. EST. As noted above, we will be live blogging that morning beginning at 9:30 a.m.

    Jack Birle, Washington Examiner.

    In June 2022, the Supreme Court ruled “in Carson v. Makin that Maine could not exclude religious schools from a state program that allows parents to use vouchers for public or private schools for their children.” Now, a group of Catholic schools has asked the justices to revisit the program and address rules that were passed while the earlier case was pending “to bar schools from participating ... if their admissions policies prefer students of a certain religion, allow religious discrimination in their schools, or do not follow the state’s views on gender ideology,” according to the Washington Examiner. “The Catholic schools urge the Supreme Court to address multiple questions if it takes up the case, including whether to overrule the 1990 Supreme Court ruling Employment Division v. Smith, which found that the free exercise clause does not allow for people to violate a law as part of their religious practice, as long as the law is valid and neutral in how it is applied. The petition ... argues that Smith has allowed Maine to continue to exclude religious schools from state programs.”.

    It has been revealed that attorneys for Emily Bickford, a Maine mother “who has been prohibited from taking her 13-year-old daughter to church” in a custody order, appealed her challenge to the order to the Supreme Court last week. The order allows the child’s father “to solely decide on his daughter’s involvement with Calvary Chapel Church.” Bickford asks the justices to find that it violates “parental rights and religious liberty protections,” according to WMTW in Portland, Maine. “A parent’s ability to take her child to church during her own parenting time now depends on the State in which she lives,” Bickford’s petition for review notes. “When a state court strips a fit parent of her right to direct her child’s religious upbringing and vests a co-parent with veto power, it deploys the coercive authority of the State to extinguish a fundamental right.”.

    Kanishka Singh and Julia Harte, Reuters.

    On Tuesday, “Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose wrongful deportation to El Salvador made him a symbol for critics of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, left the US for Spain,” according to Reuters. His voluntarily departure brought an end to “a legal fight that, at one point, reached the US Supreme Court.” It began when “US authorities sent Abrego Garcia, who entered the US illegally, to a megaprison in El Salvador in March 2025 despite a prior court order barring his return there because of the risk of persecution.” For months, officials “mentioned they could not bring him back,” but the Supreme Court ultimately “ordered the government [to] facilitate Abrego Garcia’s return.” After he returned to the United States in June 2025, Abrego Garcia faced human smuggling charges “stemming from an earlier incident” and a renewed deportation effort.

    Gavin Bade, The Wall Street Journal.

    Since February, when the Supreme Court held that President Donald Trump did not have the authority under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to impose tariffs, the Trump administration has been using other statutes to rebuild the president’s tariff regime. This week, that effort will continue when the administration confirms increased “tariffs on China and dozens of other countries,” according to The Wall Street Journal. “The new tariffs will likely be added to levies from a separate tariff action, unveiled in July, that sought to penalize nations for not blocking the trade of goods produced with forced labor,” and target countries that the Trump administration has concluded are harming U.S. producers by “flood[ing] global markets with cheaper goods.” That July action sparked a new lawsuit over the administration’s tariff policies.

    It has been revealed that on Monday, a panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit sided with President Donald Trump “in his fight to overturn his hush money criminal conviction in Newly introduced York, ruling that a judge wrongly denied his effort to move the case into federal court,” according to The Hill. Trump’s current push to transfer the case “cites the Supreme Court’s presidential immunity ruling.” The president contends that “he has the legal right to bring it up before a federal judge as a defense,” and the 2nd Circuit panel held on Monday that the district court did not properly consider this argument. “Monday’s decision effectively puts a halt to Trump’s ongoing appeal in New York’s state court system and moves it to federal court, where the president will continue pressing his arguments that the case should remain there.”.

    Philip Jankowski, The Dallas Morning News.

    Texas’ Democratic Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson noted he will not defend the state’s “Ten Commandments classroom law,” just weeks before the justices are expected to consider whether to take up a challenge to it, according to The Dallas Morning News. “My jurisprudential opinion is that the law is unconstitutional,” Johnson said. “The court will have the ultimate say as to what’s constitutional and what is not, but I’m the one who says what the state’s position is, and it will not be the position the state has previously taken.” Outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton “cited Johnson’s unwillingness to defend the law as a reason the justices should decline to hear” the challenge to it in the state’s brief in opposition, which was filed on November 10. “If the Supreme Court stays out of the fight, a federal appeals court ruling upholding the classroom displays in Texas would remain in place, preserving a legal victory for Paxton even after he leaves office in January.”.

    With just over a week remaining before the justices will hear argument in a pair of challenges to the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style semiautomatic rifles, the Supreme Court on Tuesday afternoon put off a decision on a request by Cook County, Illinois, to dismiss the dispute over its ban as moot – that is, no longer a live controversy. The court’s brief, unsigned order came one day after the justices granted a request by the lead plaintiff to remove him from the case.

    On Tuesdays for the past few months, we have dedicated the Closer Look section of this newsletter to covering the plaintiffs behind landmark Supreme Court cases. In this article, Blake took a step back and reflected on what we have learned.

    In his Empirical SCOTUS column, Adam Feldman analyzed each justice’s voting pattern in interim docket cases involving federal executive action, highlighting “a conservative majority whose members separate over particular exercises of federal power, a liberal bloc with distinguishable voting and dissent records, and occasional alliances that cross ideological lines.”.

    In his Court Beyond Borders column, Martin Flaherty focused on the Supreme Court’s grant of review in Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on President Donald Trump’s suspension of asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border. The case, according to Flaherty, will put “the Supreme Court’s wariness toward international law” in the spotlight.

    In her In Dissent column on Monday, Anastasia Boden explored 1978’s Federal Communications Commission v. Pacifica Foundation, holding that the government may “constitutionally prohibit indecency even” when it falls “short of legal obscenity.” In a dissenting opinion, Justice William Brennan criticized the majority for “attempt[ing] to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people.”.

    In a recent development, (SCOTUSblog Plus) Since joining in 2022, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson has forged a unique role on the Supreme Court. It often appears, as Amy noted in this analysis, that Jackson’s goal in dissenting opinions is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision of the law and speak to the public directly – regardless of whether anyone else on the court agrees.

    In his SCOTUSCrim column on Friday, Rory Little aimed “to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law” and explore “why that can be so interesting.”.

    Sarah Isgur and David French critique Congress’ current governing processes with the help of Michael “Frags” Fragoso, a partner at Torridon Law, and Nicholas Bagley, a professor of law at the University of Michigan and author of the book Why We Can’t Have Nice Things: How Legal Reformers Accidentally Broke America.

    The Closer Look in Wednesday editions is typically an entry in our Ask Amy series, in which Amy Howe answers reader questions about the Supreme Court.

    Q: At least for those of us of a certain age, the November 9 order list contained a familiar name in the “Attorney Discipline” section: Larry Klayman, perhaps best known as a frequent and fervent foe of the Clinton administration, had been “disbarred from the practice of law” in the Supreme Court. Which leads to the question: How, exactly, does someone get disbarred from the Supreme Court bar – especially if, like Klayman, they’ve never argued there?

    A: The answer (like so many others) can be found in the Supreme Court’s rules, starting with the rule that outlines how someone becomes eligible to join the Supreme Court bar, which is necessary not only to argue before the justices but also to sign filings there: lawyers must have been (among other things) “admitted to practice” in another jurisdiction for at least three years, and they cannot have been subject to any disciplinary proceedings during that time.

    Because becoming a member of the Supreme Court bar requires a clean disciplinary record, it follows that disciplinary problems can get a lawyer kicked out of the Supreme Court bar – even if the underlying conduct had nothing to do with the court itself. Specifically, the court’s rules provide for the suspension of any lawyer who “has been disbarred or suspended from practice in any court of record, or has engaged in conduct unbecoming a member of the Bar of this Court.” The suspended lawyer then has the chance to try to persuade the court “why disciplinary action should not be taken,” after which the court may take “any appropriate disciplinary action,” which can include disbarment.

    In Klayman’s case, he was apparently suspended by the bar associations in the District of Columbia and Florida for alleged ethical violations in connection with his efforts to represent rancher Cliven Bundy in a federal court in Nevada, leading to his disbarment from the Supreme Court earlier this month. Klayman told Law360 that he plans to seek reconsideration of the Supreme Court’s order.

    “It is like having a upcoming in-law at Thanksgiving dinner. Uncle Fred will put on a clean shirt.”.

    — Chief Justice John Roberts’ thoughts when a new member joins the Supreme Court.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.
